title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
body_text: Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud | Scott's Blog Scott J. Goldman Posts RSS Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud November 11, 2026 16 min read Nice enough air purifier, but I don’t love the app. The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime: My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one : The venerable Coway Airmega It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality. This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep. The Good Night button # Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume. The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS ). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of). The Coway Airmega IconS The existing Home Assistant integration # Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant . The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà! Coway IoCare cloud Coway's servers, somewhere on the internet commands ↑ status ↓ status ↑ commands ↓ My house Home Assistant IoCare integration Air purifier Airmega IconS, on Wi-Fi Apple Home the Good Night button Why ditch the cloud? # The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks. Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break: Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it. Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well. Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it. Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device. Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban. On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows). A way in # I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server. Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one. All that said, two major things have changed. First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys. Ian Carroll @iangcarroll For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices! 10:15 AM · Oct 20, 2026 So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it. The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes. Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud. Our man in the middle # Initially, I tried to set it up like this: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution? The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi, same room Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic Ethernet My laptop Internet Sharing, bridging Wi-Fi to Ethernet Wi-Fi My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet Next, we need to configure the Pi. I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes. Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions. After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with: scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8 set client_interfaces { # handle 4 type ifname elements = { "wlan0" } } chain prerouting { # handle 1 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6 } chain input { # handle 2 type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7 iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8 iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13 iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14 iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15 } chain forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16 oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18 iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19 } } table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12 chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2 } chain filter_forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept; ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5 ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6 iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7 iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8 oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9 } } Basically, the masquerade rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the redirect rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of mitmproxy . Also on the Pi, mitmproxy runs with its web interface, mitmweb , using a command line like this: mitmweb \ --mode transparent --showhost \ --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \ --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \ --set web_open_browser=false \ --emudhra-old Yes, off the shelf, mitmproxy has a built-in option ( --emudhra-old ) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic. Snooping on the fan # Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Pi-MITM-Test Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the mitmproxy web interface: So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request . The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list. Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all. mitmproxy has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in mitmproxy ’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic. """Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device.""" from pathlib import Path from mitmproxy import ctx, http def response (flow: http . HTTPFlow) -> None : if ( flow . client_conn . peername[ 0 ] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP and flow . request . scheme == "http" and flow . request . method == "GET" and flow . request . pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com" and flow . request . path . split( "?" , 1 )[ 0 ] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem" and flow . response is not None and flow . response . status_code == 200 ): certificate = Path( "/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem" ) . read_bytes() flow . response = http . Response . make( 200 , certificate, { "Content-Type" : "application/x-pem-file" , "Cache-Control" : "no-store" , }, ) flow . metadata[ "coway_test_ca_served" ] = True ctx . log . info( "Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request" ) Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests: Hypothesis confirmed We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able. The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run tcpdump on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices. Going back to the POST in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned: { "header": { "success": true, "result": "S1000", "message": "SUCCESS" }, "payload": { "macAddr": "<redacted>", "certToken": "<redacted>", "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com", "port": 8883, "serial": "<redacted>", "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0", "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem", "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key", "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt", "svcCode": "002AIR007", "countryCd": "US" } } So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is. For now, we can write another mitmproxy plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. mitmproxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream: The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now… and after a few minutes… There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway. Bluetooth setup process # When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way. I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before . My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it , and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode. Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C. This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs. Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via adb , look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs. After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this: Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic FFA0 (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address. Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic FFA2 : "P001" + protobuf { command: 1, key: Base64(random_letters) } Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address. Build the configuration payload, which looks like this: { "cmd": 2, "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi", "pwd": "example-wifi-password", "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF", "type": 1, "macAddr": "112233445566", "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem", "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0", "certToken": "example-enrollment-token", "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001" } That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to FFA2 as well. Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes. The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script. I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload ( caUrl and certSvrUrl ). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration. Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan. Home Assistant integration # Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan . My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly. After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant. And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home. All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night. If you liked this post, I can email you when I write another one. Subscribe I don't post that often, so it won't be much email. title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
body_text: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell | Joshka.net joshka.net writing about resume projects github linkedin mastodon bluesky x soundcloud building: ratatui betamax jk ratatui-diff practice all projects → Terminal borders that don't cost a cell 2026-11-13 :: tags:  #Ghostty   #Ratatui   #TUI   #Terminals This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab. I maintain Ratatui , so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us. Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about this. The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough: So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors. Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded. Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters: Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets. What I'd use it for Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side. Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top. Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge. Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text. Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it. Up close The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback: The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame: Charts Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui: And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines: In motion Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog: Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here: Show the cell grid What box characters can't do The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that. Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration. You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included. Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways. How it works A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors. The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( ▖▗▘▝ and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time. The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them. Styles and joints Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it. When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor. The wire format Everything is one DCS string with a namespace: ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \ The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders: ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \ bottom edge, blue: an underline hello ESC [ 0 m SGR 0 clears the pen There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS. The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope. Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible. The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer. Prior art Parts of this have been done before: DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color. SGR 51 to 65 : framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge. The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses and X/Open curses ( WA_TOP , WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves. IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields. What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol. My own first prototype was in Rio ( raphamorim/rio#1947 ), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that. The awkward (edge) cases When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed. Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them. Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in. Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell. On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB. Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on. Try it The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode): git clone - b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git cd ghostty zig build - Doptimize=ReleaseFast - Dxcframework-target=native open zig-out/Ghostty.app Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation: python3 scripts/cell-borders.py # the default view python3 scripts/cell-borders.py - -styles # line styles, joints and outside fill Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag ( --placement , --styles and so on) if you want to start on it. The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch . It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above: git clone - b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git cd ratatui cargo run - p tiling-panes Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are. The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop: To run it: cargo run - p cell-border-top It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency. What I'd like to hear I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion , or on Hacker News and Lobsters . Thanks for reading! body_text: Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally | Unsloth Documentation Skip to content Introducing Unsloth Desktop: the first local app to run & train models ✨ Read more ⌘ Ctrl k GitBook Assistant Ask Reddit Discord GitHub Newsletter More 🇺🇸 English GitBook Assistant GitBook Assistant GitBook Assistant I'm here to help you with the docs. This page is also available as Markdown . GitBook Assistant Ask On this page Models Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally Guide to running Qwen3.8 quants including Qwen3.8-27B on your local setup. Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop . Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models. Run Qwen3.8 Guide Download Unsloth Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include: Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex MTP enabled for fast inference Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more Unsloth quants: Qwen3.8- 27B -GGUF Dynamic 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B in Unsloth Desktop Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026) We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat. Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better! We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1 , and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. We used 256K context lengths for all agentic benchmarks, and 128K for the rest. We followed the same methodology for Qwen3.8-27B as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next which also utilized our V3.1 preview algorithm. Dynamic V3.1 Full Breakdown Click below to see full details of benchmarking and more: Click to expand Full details and breakdown Exllama-v3 considerations To compare GSQ-RCO and Exllama-v3, we had to exclude the token embedding layer from the x axis, as Exllama-v3 uses BF16 for it. If you consider the full download size and total RAM usage for Exllama-v3, then adding the BF16 embedding table and including all embedding sizes changes the plots. Our main plots's x axis removes the embedding layer sizes from all quant providers. However on pure RAM usage and disk space usage vs accuracy, the below plot is the true reflection of actual usage. We have not investigated why Exllama-v3 keeps token embeddings in BF16, but as the lm_head is still quantized heavily, the embedding layer might have "absorbed" most of the quantization damage from it. We would be glad to benchmark new Exllama-v3 non BF16 token embedding quants like using 8-bit for example, and see if benchmarks change. GSQ-RCO results are misleading For LiveCodeBench, GSQ-RCO showed Unsloth UD3 quants doing consistently worse than ISTA's. However we found the opposite - UD3 quants (our OLD quants) do better than ISTA on LCB on all sizes except the smallest. UD3.1 further improves on LCB as well. We approximate that GSQ-RCO used a context budget of 96K, as that best fits the data for the runs we have. At 96K, GSQ-RCO does somewhat do better than UD3, but at 128K, UD3 does much better. On another benchmark, for ISTA GSQ-RCO's AIME25 benchmarks, their quants reach 100%, 100%, 100% and 96.7% accuracy recovery. And they said our quants do worse. Through out investigations, we estimate ISTA only did 1 trial - we did 14 trials, and we show on average the recovery rate is 93% to 96% - not 100% accuracy recovery. And in fact our UD3 old quants do BETTER on average than their quants on 14 runs vs 1 run of theirs , so we draw the opposite conclusion if you run the trials more. We also checked and graded our answers using Math Verify Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs and also LightEval and we find exactly the same conclusions. We also tried greedy decoding (temperature of 0), and this could not get the 100% accuracy recovery ISTA found across multiple greedy runs, as GPUs themselves are non deterministic. That is why you benchmarks should be run multiple times. Greedy decoding is also not representative of real world use cases. We also checked 96K (which is most likely ISTA's budget) and 128K, and our quants still do on average better. KLD of Unsloth v3.1 vs v3 We did KLD for multiple domains for Unsloth UD3.1 quants and UD3 quants - we reduce KLD throughout most quants and most domains - we did not replace the 3-bit ones, as we found UD3 to do mostly great, and the accuracy recovery on benchmarks was not significant enough with UD3.1 to warrant an update, so we did not update them. Benchmark details and setups We follow the same procedure for all benchmarks as for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as well as discussed in Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs . Extra high is enabled by default so if you want shorter thinking traces, you can adjust the thinking effort : Parameter Thinking Mode Instruct (non-thinking) Mode temperature 1.0 0.7 top_p 0.95 0.80 top_k 20 20 min_p 0.0 0.0 presence_penalty 0.0 1.5 repetition_penalty 1.0 1.0 Maximum context window: 262,144 (can be extended to 1M via YaRN) Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0 , top_p=0.95 , top_k=20 , min_p=0.0 , presence_penalty=0.0 , repetition_penalty=1.0 Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7 , top_p=0.80 , top_k=20 , min_p=0.0 , presence_penalty=1.5 , repetition_penalty=1.0 💡 Thinking + Preserve Thinking Qwen3.8 has Preserve Thinking which leaves the thinking trace from the previous conversation. This increases the number of tokens you use, but could increase accuracy in continued conversations. Unsloth has 'Think' and Preserved Thinking toggles for Qwen3.8 (see right): Qwen3.8-27B comes with support for reasoning_effort , which can be used to adjust reasoning depth and control cost. These toggles are automatically enabled in Unsloth: xhigh (default): for complex tasks demanding thorough analysis medium : balancing accuracy and speed low : efficient reasoning optimizing for speed and cost none To change thinking / reasoning effort in unsloth run or llama-server , use --chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"medium"}' If you're on Windows Powershell, use: --chat-template-kwargs "{\"reasoning_effort\":\"medium\"}" Change medium to your desired reasoning level. title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
body_text: FAA lifts ground stop hours after stranding thousands of flights across the U.S. IE 11 is not supported. For an optimal experience visit our site on another browser. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Duffy details timeline of ground stop, demands more FAA funding 06:00 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 13, 2026, 4:09 PM EST / Updated Nov. 14, 2026, 1:56 AM EST By Corky Siemaszko , Tom Costello , Joy Y. Wang and Marlene Lenthang Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday. By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware. The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights. A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment. What caused the ground stop Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack. “FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage. Why disruptions continued Saturday Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush. But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News. Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded. “At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’” Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off. DHS says nationwide ground stop was not a cyberattack: 'We are built to handle crisis like this' 02:31 Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years. In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage. Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported. Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said. Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X . Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday. Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations. Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty “Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.” With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing. There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage. Frustrated Chicago travelers seeking answers on checked bags amid nationwide ground stop 02:41 Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history. After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports. In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers. Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time . Phil Brink · Monday, November 09, 2026 NVIDIA's headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Authorities are investigating the reported theft of $11.4 million in NVIDIA computer hardware during a shipment from Oakland to Texas. (Photo: NVIDIA) Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments. According to The Mercury News , the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations. Oakland police confirm investigation The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement: “The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.” The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded. Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance. In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding , from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case. Why it matters The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation. He owned and operated a freight brokerage for more than a decade before organized fraud targeted his business, forcing him to rethink how freight companies identify and manage risk. The lessons he learned continue to shape his reporting, education and collaboration with brokers, carriers, shippers and law enforcement. He developed FreightWaves' Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) program to give transportation professionals practical knowledge and a structured framework for identifying and managing fraud risk. title: AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
body_text: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths | Mathematics | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 3 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock Mathematics ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems Alex Bellos Fri 13 Nov 2026 11.38 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 13.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age. After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science. Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it. Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought. View image in fullscreen Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive “I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.” Did you solve it? Gödel’s incompleteness theorem Read more Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation. In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978. Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team. In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature. “In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts. “The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice. Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes. The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern. “What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.” Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.” In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].” Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.” Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.” Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.” Explore more on these topics Mathematics AI (artificial intelligence) Finland Europe Austria news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies. title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
body_text: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models — Haddy Alchaer Haddy Alchaer World models · JEPA · Planning After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models By Haddy Alchaer · November 2026 Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra training 0 / 24 on target · step 0 Vanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved. There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1] The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions. The three parts of a JEPA world model. This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2] , a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3] , a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it. A goal image from Push-T The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics. The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning. Success on 250 long-horizon tasks 78 % Vanilla LeWM learned predictor ≈ 77 % LeWM real physics the simulator itself That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went. Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did. 1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%. So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks. 250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps away LeWM, all 75 steps at once as published 22% Exact physics, all 75 steps at once the simulator itself 42% +20 LeWM given a new subgoal every 25 steps same model, shorter hops 80% +58 0 25 50 75 100% Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together. LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 steps Plan all 75 steps at once ... one search, far goal 22% A subgoal every 25 steps ... three short searches 80% Chaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate. This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics. Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together. The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence. 2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals. This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach. The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the same score received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right? Planning through a memory of demonstrations start goal Jumps are free · 8 jumps · 62% Each jump has a cost · 1 jump · 85% Each thin path is one demonstration. With free jumps, the shortest route hops between demonstrations into a path the block can't physically follow. With a cost per jump, it stays on them. The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration. demonstrations, all ending in about the same place goals in the standard test goals from other demonstrations The standard test picks its goals along these streams. The harder test asks for goals like the orange ones, which no single demonstration leads to. The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure. That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap. 3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%. Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%). Filling a gap in memory with transformed demonstrations a demonstration segment from elsewhere the same segment, shifted, rotated or mirrored Block reached its target, 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) 93% full memory 32% states near the goal deleted 85% gap filled with rotated and mirrored copies On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%. Harder test, by where the goal lies about 83 tasks per row Goal lies with the flow of the demonstrations 69% Goal lies across it 39% 54% Goal lies against it 27% 46% 0 25 50 75 100% success rate plain memory with transformed segments 4. The cost was “wrong” I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image. The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too. To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s. Block held on target, same 50 tasks exact-physics planner Block and pusher 9 / 50 Block only 39 / 50 success with either cost 30  succeed only without the pusher 0  succeed only with the pusher included Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from how the goal was created . The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve. Pusher included vs. not Cost compares the block and the pusher Cost compares the block only target for the block where the goal image put the pusher Replay But LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining. Sixteen versions of one goal A predicted end state 16 copies of the goal with the pusher moved, and the closest one sets the cost This applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end. The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for. What comes next None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost. The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4] , which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T. Hierarchical subgoal planner on top of LeWM demonstrations in memory subgoals taken from memory a goal beyond the data Going in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer . References [1] Y. LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence . OpenReview, 2022. [2] L. Maes, Q. Le Lidec, D. Scieur, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, LeWorldModel: Stable End-to-End Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture from Pixels . arXiv:2603.19312, 2026. [3] C. Chi et al., Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion . RSS, 2023. [4] W. Zhang, B. Terver, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning . arXiv:2610.06805, 2026. © 2026 Haddy Alchaer
