A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem
body_text: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem - Haskell Foundation - Haskell Community = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Haskell Community A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem Haskell Foundation hasufell November 13, 2026, 5:03am 1 Hi all, the technical leadership committee of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped! We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational. We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives. We tried to keep the community proposal process as light as possible. However, we believe that fairness and participation are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback. Below is our vision. Feel free to get in touch with us! The TLC’s shared vision We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation: It is good for humans to write by hand: Type safety, powerful abstractions and referential transparency have enabled engineers all over the world in startups and big tech to deliver and maintain complex systems. It is good for responsible AI workflows: review is a significant bottleneck in modern AI-workflows and Haskell’s strengths heavily favor the reviewer. Additionally, the ability to quickly design eDSLs and express constraints where it matters allows to set up strong guardrails for code generation, without losing flexibility. There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly. We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone: Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity Industry: focussing on stability and scaling A vision of productivity Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance! Iteration speed Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows. While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2. Debugging and profiling Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries: live step-through debugging actually useful stack traces beautiful performance analysis reports And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP). Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase. Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools. Onboarding and DevX In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole. installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as: write programs that do one thing and do it well write programs that work together write programs that are extensible Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans. A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost. To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to: have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations build a robust cryptography library stack harden our supply chain We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell . A vision of stability What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes? While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway. The questions we need to answer along the way are: how can users opt out of breaking changes? how long can we keep support windows open? how can we make the upgrade experience better? Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn. We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem. A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other. We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world. We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values. 83 Likes 6d03 November 13, 2026, 12:10pm 2 Thank you @hasufell and the TLC for writing this up; it’s very inspiring to see these goals. I think this ambitious agenda will provide us with a lot of fun and profit. 5 Likes Elland November 13, 2026, 7:26pm 3 That’s really great to see I’ll be doing my part and see if I can submit a proposal for some unglamorous work I’ve been meaning to do. 4 Likes dawkrish November 13, 2026, 10:55pm 4 Woah, this is so inspiring and motivating! I have multiple features I want to add to HLS! Is Haskell Team finally focusing on “Adoption” ? 2 Likes OlaoluwaM November 14, 2026, 12:12am 5 Is there a place to sign up to be a volunteer, or is it just the general “help out where you can”? 1 Like simonmic November 14, 2026, 12:22am 6 Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50484235 5 Likes wiz November 14, 2026, 9:29am 7 Don’t start reading without your hypertension pills! Lots of moronic and sloppy takes. 4 Likes tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 2:26pm 8 hasufell: We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture Can I suggest we do this by promoting the use of effect systems to this end? Effect systems are basically capability systems if you generalise the definition of each of those two terms in a natural way, as I explain in my article Bluefin is a capability system . Capability systems have a long history of development for security purposes. Haskell is the natural setting for capability systems, as it is referentially transparent, which capability systems proponents would describe as “having no ambient authority”. prophet November 14, 2026, 3:28pm 9 In what way would Bluefin have any security advantages over plain IO? My understanding is that the security benefits of capability systems usually fall into two camps: OS-level capabilities like FreeBSD’s pledge stop any code (including code from an RCE vulnerability) from performing operations it’s not supposed to. Library level capabilities (like the object capibilities in Pony you mentioned) can mitigate supply chain vulnerabilities by stopping dependencies from calling any code that does more than they need. 1 doesn’t apply to Bluefin and 2 can be trivially circumvented by using unsafePerformIO 1 Like tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 3:52pm 10 To be clear, I’m not suggesting Bluefin specifically as the solution to secure design and architecture, I’m saying that that one benefit Haskell has that will help with secure design and architecture is effect systems in general . In the world of effect systems, Bluefin and effectful have a number of non-security-related benefits that I’ve elaborated in detail elsewhere, but they don’t have an inherent security advantage, per se. I’m not too familiar with pledge , but I don’t think it’s a capability system. I think it just acts to reduce ambient authority. A capability system allows you to run different components of your program with different levels of authority, in a fine grained way, based on what capabilities are in scope in each of those components. Regarding your point 2, yes, effect systems can do that, but of course the dependencies would have to be written with that use case in mind (as they do in Pony, unless I’m much mistaken). Sure, you can circumvent anything with unsafePerformIO , as it allows you to write unsafeCoerce and thereby walk over your entire heap making arbitrary changes. I’m not proposing that Haskell would be a verified system (although I’d be interested to see how close to one it could become with SafeHaskell ). 1 Like prophet November 14, 2026, 4:08pm 11 I’m not too familiar with pledge , but I don’t think it’s a capability system That’s fair. Fuchsia capabilities are probably a better example. Regarding your point 2, yes, effect systems can do that, but of course the dependencies would have to be written with that use case in mind (as they do in Pony, unless I’m much mistaken). Well, the difference is that (AIUI) pony doesn’t have any escape hatches and so if a function doesn’t receive a capability to, say, access the file system, it literally cannot do so. No matter how fancy your effect system is, a compromised Haskell dependency can always call unsafePerformIO (writeFile ... malware) . I just don’t see any concrete security vulnerabilities that could be avoided by using an effect system. I don’t disagree that effect systems can have benefits for software engineering in general, but I really don’t see how they’re relevant to “secure design and architecture”. tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 4:19pm 12 prophet: That’s fair. Fuchsia capabilities are probably a better example. OK, and what do you see as the fundamental distinction between Fuchsia and Haskell-with-an-effect-system (besides one being an operating system and the other having an additional level of “nesting” within a programming language)? I can only repeat that I’m not proposing that Haskell would be a verified system. Nonetheless, I think a software project written in a capability system, albeit not a formally verified one, would still be easier to implement correctly and audit that one written in the style of “ambient authority”. I would be interested to hear your arguments against that, if you disagree. Regarding Pony, perhaps it always enforces the equivalent of SafeHaskell . I would interested to know where you think “ SafeHaskell plus effect systems” would fall short of providing “secure design and architecture”. Perhaps a mod should split this off into its own topic? 2 Likes Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

title: Rust 1.100
body_text: Announcing Rust 1.100.0 | Rust Blog Rust Blog Rust Install Learn Tools Governance Community 🖌 Light Dark System Announcing Rust 1.100.0 Nov. 12, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup , you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0 . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel ( rustup default beta ) or the nightly channel ( rustup default nightly ). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss associated function [1] which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases. Stabilized APIs impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for Vec<T, A> impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &[T] impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &mut [T] std::alloc::Allocator std::alloc::Global std::alloc::System impl Allocator for Global impl Allocator for System impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Box<T, A> impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &mut A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Arc<T, A> impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Rc<T, A> Box::new_in Box::from_raw_in Box::from_non_null_in Box::into_raw_with_allocator Box::into_non_null_with_allocator Box::allocator Vec::new_in Vec::with_capacity_in Vec::from_raw_parts_in Vec::from_parts_in Vec::into_raw_parts_with_allocator Vec::into_parts_with_allocator Vec::allocator Child::main_thread_handle impl Default for std::sync::Once bool::toggle Box::take Box::map Rc::map Arc::map impl AsRef<T> for ! impl AsMut<T> for ! core::mem::DropGuard core::mem::conjure_zst UnsafeCell::replace UnsafeCell::as_ref_unchecked UnsafeCell::as_mut_unchecked str::trim_prefix str::trim_suffix [T]::trim_prefix [T]::trim_suffix Path::trim_prefix Vec::from_fn os::windows::process::CommandExt::show_window Other changes Check out everything that changed in Rust , Cargo , and Clippy . Contributors to 1.100.0 Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks! it has deliberately been chosen not to be a method to avoid name collisions with the DerefMut -enabled method resolution on the inner type. ↩ Get help! Turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and create designs with AI agents via MCP. zigzag.diy/ Topics brother-skitch embroidery embroidery-digitizing embroidery-software machine-embroidery macos mcp model-context-protocol rust svg vector-editor windows Resources Readme Apache-2.0 license Activity Stars 737 stars Watchers 6 watching Forks 37 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 11 Commits 11 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date .github/ workflows .github/ workflows examples examples packaging packaging src src vendor vendor .gitignore .gitignore CHANGELOG.md CHANGELOG.md Cargo.lock Cargo.lock Cargo.toml Cargo.toml LICENSE LICENSE NOTICE NOTICE README.md README.md RELEASE.md RELEASE.md THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md build.rs build.rs View all files Repository files navigation README Apache-2.0 license More items ZigZag Visit zigzag.diy ZigZag is a visual embroidery editor built in Rust for performance, with built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) support so AI agents can create and edit designs alongside you. Turn SVG artwork into stitches, fine-tune it in the editor, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF, or VP3 for broad compatibility with embroidery machines—or send designs directly to a Brother Skitch (PP1) over Bluetooth . Draw in Illustrator, draw in ZigZag, or let an agent draw. The Rust engine and zigzag command-line tool power the same workflow outside the editor. See ZigZag in action zigzag-demo.mp4 Stitching on a Brother Skitch (PP1) Download the video (MP4, 1080p) · Original post on X . Download for Mac Download ZigZag.dmg For Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, macOS 11 or later. Open the DMG, then drag ZigZag into Applications. The release is signed and notarized by Apple. No Rust installation is needed. Or with Homebrew : brew install --cask simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag To update a Homebrew installation: brew upgrade --cask --greedy simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag Starting with version 0.1.3, ZigZag also offers an in-app updater: it tells you when there's a newer release and installs it when you say (ZigZag › Check for Updates…). Download for Windows Download ZigZag for Windows — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-windows.zip asset on the latest release. For 64-bit Windows 10 (version 1709 or later) and Windows 11. Unzip it and double-click ZigZag.exe . Windows SmartScreen warns on apps without a Microsoft-trusted signature the first time they run; click More info → Run anyway . No Rust installation is needed. Download for Linux Download ZigZag for Linux — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-linux.tar.gz asset on the latest release. For x86-64 Linux desktops with glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+), X11 or Wayland, and OpenGL. Extract the archive and run ./zigzag-studio inside the extracted folder. It also includes the zigzag CLI and zigzag-mcp bridge; no Rust installation is needed. See the included README.txt for runtime dependencies and Bluetooth setup. Release notes and checksums · Changelog · Publishing a release zigzag/ src/svg.rs SVG import (usvg): fill and stroke parts, transforms, text src/document/ editable document; settings saved back into SVG ids, layout edits as SVG transforms, lettering src/params.rs stitch settings tokens + fabric presets src/stitch/fill.rs tatami fill (scanline sections, staggered rows) src/stitch/satin.rs satin columns: two rails, auto-satin, underlays, short stitches, lean src/stitch/columns.rs shapes that branch or have holes, cut into satin columns src/stitch/stroke.rs running / triple-run stitch src/boolean.rs polygon booleans and offsets (i_overlay) src/design.rs planner: overlap removal, cap order, routing, trims src/route.rs travel out of sight: a way through fills and under what covers src/checks.rs digitizing checks (sizes, widths, lettering, hoop) src/machine/profile.rs machine profiles: hoops and file format, built in (profiles.json) or your own src/formats/ PES (+PEC), DST, EXP, JEF, VP3, Skitch PEN writers; PES/PEC/DST/EXP/JEF readers; preview; worksheet src/machine/ Skitch Bluetooth protocol (+ btleplug client, `ble` feature) src/studio/ editor (egui on OpenGL via glow) + MCP server (`gui` feature) src/mcp_bridge.rs stdio ↔ HTTP bridge for MCP clients that launch a command Build cargo build --release # CLI + MCP bridge, no system deps cargo build --release --features gui,ble # + the studio editor and Skitch upload Linux needs the usual X11/Wayland and OpenGL dev libraries for gui . libdbus is vendored for ble . Stitch types Type What it does Works on Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; stitches square across or leaning ( lean=8 ); several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes : rings use inner/outer outline, bars and crescents split at their tips, letters and other shapes that branch or have a counter are cut into columns where the branches part (a P into its stem and bowl, a T into bar and stem), or border follows the outline Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser). Planner features: Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap). Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering. Routing: travel stitches stay out of sight: straight across where a straight line stays inside the fill, otherwise round the inside of its outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), otherwise any way through the fill (round its holes, through its necks), under a satin that's about to be sewn, or under whatever is sewn later on top. An object's last piece is sewn toward the end the next object can be reached from. So satin lettering sewn stroke by stroke needs cuts only between letters when each stroke is followed by one that covers the way to it (a T's stem before its bar; an E's bars before its stem). A fill in separate parts is sewn part by part, each part's underlay and top together. So a fill with cut-outs, or a dither in scattered blocks under another color, is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where none of that works (up to 50 mm of travel). Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). What's left to cut is the document's Connect bar: drag it to sew across gaps up to N mm (between objects, or the parts of one) with running stitches instead of cuts. Those stitches show, so the panel counts the cuts saved as you drag and the canvas lights up what would be sewn. Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit. Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit. Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering. Mac app On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ): packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized --release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain: xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag . For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp . Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch. Studio The approved embroidered icons live in packaging/macos/AppIcon.png (light) and packaging/macos/AppIcon-dark.png (dark). The Mac build regenerates both multi-resolution .icns files; run bash packaging/macos/make-icons.sh to regenerate them separately. Finder and the unopened app use the light icon. While the studio is running, its Dock icon follows the app's light/dark theme, including the ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark override. zigzag-studio [design.svg | logo.png] [--mcp-port 7878 | --no-mcp | --mcp-stdio] Laid out like Illustrator, styled like a Mac app: Tools down the left edge: Select (V), Direct Selection (A), Hand (H), Pen (P): click for corners, drag for curves (Option breaks the handles, Shift keeps 45°, Space moves the point being placed); while drawing, Option lends it the Anchor Point tool (drag a segment to bend it, a handle to move it alone, click a smooth point for a corner) and ⌘ lends Direct Selection (drag a point or handle, then keep drawing), and on a selected path Option-drag bends a segment too. Illustrator's Pen group is behind it: Add Anchor Point (+) clicks a point onto an outline without changing its shape, Delete Anchor Point (-) clicks one out (Option swaps the two while held), and Anchor Point (Shift+C) converts points between smooth and corner and drags one handle alone. Press and hold the Pen (or right-click it) for the group's flyout, Option-click it to step through the group, or tear the group off into a toolbar of its own with the strip at the flyout's edge; the Shape tools work the same way. Brush (B), with VectorCraft's path clean-up tools in its group: Smooth (drag along a path to take the wobble out: fewer points, smoother curves; Smoothness in the bar above), Path Eraser (drag across a path to cut that part away) and Join (scrub between two open ends to join them, or an open path's two ends to close it). Shapes (M rectangle, L ellipse, \ line; hold or right-click for polygon and star), Fill Angle (G), Measure (I), Text (T). Below them, the selection's thread swatch: click it for the thread color picker. Curves, the Illustrator way: the Pen clicks corners and click-drags curves (Option while dragging breaks the handle for a sharp turn; Shift keeps points and handles at 45°; hold Space to move the point you're placing). Click the last point to make it a corner, or drag from it to start the next curve in a new direction. Click the first point to close a shape; Enter, Esc, ⌘-click or another tool ends a line and keeps it. With a path selected, the Pen continues it from an open end, adds a point on its outline, deletes a point you click, and Option-click turns a point corner ↔ smooth (Option-drag pulls out new handles). While drawing, click another open path's end to join the two into one. The cursor shows what a click will do. Direct Selection drags points and handles of any shape from your SVG (circles and rects become paths); dragging a curve bends it under the pointer (Option-drag bends a straight one; a plain drag moves it); Delete removes points, arrows nudge them. Smart guides while drawing (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U): Pen points, shape corners and dragged points land on other objects' anchors and centers, where two outlines cross, on an outline, on 45° rays from the last point (level and upright handles too), or in line with any of those, with a magenta label saying which ("anchor", "intersect", "path", "align"…). With Shift, a point keeps its 45° angle and slides into line with the nearest target. Round corners: in Direct Selection a small circle sits inside each sharp corner; drag it in to round the corners (the selected points', or all of them), each only as far as its sides allow. Object › Path › Round Corners… does the same with a radius and Round, Inverted or Chamfer, previewed live. Brush (B), after Illustrator's Paintbrush: paint a line freehand and it comes out smooth, sewn as a satin column at the width you set (or as a running stitch). Smoothness takes out the hand's wobble; sharp turns stay sharp; end where you began to close the line. The cursor is a circle as wide as the satin. Shapes, the Illustrator way: Rectangle (M), Ellipse (L), Polygon, Star and Line (\). Drag from a corner; Option draws from the center, Shift makes a square or circle, keeps a polygon or star upright and a line at 45°. While dragging a polygon or star, ↑/↓ add or remove sides or points. Click without dragging to type an exact size. The bar at the top of the canvas switches shapes and sets corner radius, sides, points and the star's inner radius. Closed shapes come in as fills, lines as runs, in the current thread. Path tools: Object › Pathfinder (Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude; also buttons in the Transform panel when two or more objects are selected) and Object › Path (Offset Path…, Add Outline, Outline Stroke, Simplify…, Round Corners…, Clean Up…). Simplify… is VectorCraft's slider, from fewest points to closest to the original, previewed live, with Auto-Simplify picking the level for the selection's size. Clean Up… removes stray points, objects too small to sew (under 1 mm by default) and extra points (points on top of each other, points in the middle of straight lines), showing how many of each it found first. Results come back as smooth curves with their real corners (least-squares curve fitting), not as many-sided polygons. Logos from images (Image Trace): open, drop or place a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF and the Trace Image window traces it into flat-color shapes, previewed on your hat's color. Choose how many colors (or Auto), the width, detail and the smallest speck to keep; remove the white background; snap every color to your Brother, Janome or own palette's threads; and sew thin lines as single lines. Flat logos trace exactly (edges placed to a fraction of a pixel, corners restored, circles and straight lines exact); photos are posterized. The command line traces too: zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes . Contextual task bar: under the selection, the next things you'd do: its stitch type, its thread, Edit Points, Round Corners, Simplify, Unite (two or more), Duplicate. View › Contextual Task Bar (or its ••• menu) hides it. Ask an agent: the Agent panel (full height in the left dock; the sparkle at the bottom of the tool strip opens and closes it, and ⌘K or Window › Ask Agent… opens it with the prompt ready) runs Claude Code or Codex in the background, connected to this studio's MCP server, so you watch it build the design. It can only use the design tools (no shell, no file edits). The transcript shows what it said and each step, with a spinner on the one running (the one place it's shown; collapse the panel and its header shows the step and the time instead). On the canvas, the objects it's working on get a moving outline, a shimmer and a label saying what it's doing (Drawing, Placing, Restyling…), for any agent connected over MCP, not just the panel's. The panel is named for the agent (Claude Code or Codex; switch in its ≡ menu); + in its header starts a new chat, Stop ends a run. Uses the claude or codex command you've already signed in to. Like any panel it can float, join another as a tab or dock right; sharing a dock it sits at the bottom, under a divider you drag to give it more room. Thread colors and palettes: the picker shows the nearest Brother/Janome thread, a palette to click (Brother, Janome or your own), and a small custom color field. Make palettes from scratch, from the design, or from a thread kit you own (the palette's ≡ menu › New Palette from Thread Kit: Brother's 12, 40 and 22 color sets, or 40 + 22 for all 61; then Match All keeps a design to the threads in your box), add the selection's thread with +, right-click to remove; they're remembered between launches. Threads panel: the design's threads in sewing order (each color block numbered, with its stitches, and "stop" where the same thread comes twice running) or By Color (each thread once, with how many objects use it). Click a row to select what it sews; click a swatch to change that block's thread, or in By Color that thread everywhere. Group Colors and the count of color changes and trims are under the list. The panel's ≡ menu has Match All to the chosen palette, and Show Palette puts a palette to click under the list (off by default, since the thread picker has the same palettes). Simplify Design (Object › Simplify Design…, or Simplify… in the Threads panel): make a design quicker to sew. Merge the threads most alike down to a number (each pair becomes the one that sews more, so they stay real threads), take out details too small to sew well, sew across short gaps instead of trimming, sew each thread together, and (if you choose) unite layers that touch in one thread into one shape, so nothing is sewn under or between them: only the ones sewn the same way (a satin on a fill stays), or all of them. It previews on the canvas as you drag, with threads, thread changes, trims, stitches and sewing time before and after beside the controls; OK is one undo step. Panels, the Illustrator way: the Agent has the left dock to itself; Layers, Stitch, Transform, Lettering, Threads and Document are on the right. The design's issues are in the status bar (bottom right): a warning sign with a count, or a check when all's well; click it (or Window › Issues) for the list, each linked to its object. Drag a panel by its header to reorder it, move it to the other dock, or drop it on the canvas to float it (each panel's ≡ menu also has Dock Left / Dock Right / Float). Drop a panel on another panel's header and they share it as tabs; drag a tab out (or use Separate in the ≡ menu) to part them, drag the header to move the group. » at the top of a dock collapses it to a strip of icons for a bigger canvas: click an icon and the panel flies out beside the strip (drag an icon to move that panel). Click a header to collapse a panel; Window › Reset Panels puts everything back. The layout is remembered. Rename an object: double-click its name in the Layers list, as in Illustrator; Enter keeps the name, Escape doesn't. A single click only selects. Tabs, one per document (as in VectorCraft and Illustrator): Open, drop or New opens a file in a tab of its own over the canvas (the empty document you start with makes way for the first one); a file that's already open just comes forward. Each tab keeps its own undo history, selection, zoom and stitches. Click a tab to switch, ⌃Tab / ⌃⇧Tab (or Window › Next / Previous Document) to step through them, drag one to reorder, middle-click or its × (or File › Close, ⌘W) to close it; + opens a new document and » lists every tab when they don't all fit. A dot in place of the × marks unsaved changes, and closing such a tab asks whether to save it first. Right-click a tab for Close Other Tabs and Copy Path. Quitting with unsaved changes asks too (Save, or Save All for several; Don't Save; Cancel), as VectorCraft does, though not saving loses nothing: every tab comes back next time, each with its unsaved changes, and the files stay as they were until you save. Lock and hide: every row of the Layers list has an eye and a lock (Illustrator's Layers columns; Option-click for every other object, and Object › Lock ⌘2, Unlock All, Hide ⌘3, Show All). A hidden object isn't shown or sewn; a locked one can't be selected or moved, so a background stays put while you work on what's over it. Drag the Selection tool over empty canvas for a selection box; two-finger scroll, Space-drag or the Hand tool moves the canvas. Updates itself: ZigZag looks at its latest release on GitHub when it opens, and the toolbar shows an Update button when there's a newer one. On a Mac, Install and Relaunch downloads it, checks it against the release's checksum and Apple's code signature (it has to be signed by the same developer as the copy that's running), swaps it in and reopens with your documents as they were. ZigZag › Check for Updates… looks on demand; Settings › General turns the automatic look off. Windows and Linux are told and taken to the download. Travel stays out of sight: the thread gets from one part of an object to the next under stitches still to come or under what's sewn on top; a fill's sections are sewn in the order that allows it. Where there's no such way the thread is cut, or (Document panel › Travel › Sew over fill) sewn over the fill already there, which saves cuts and shows. The checks say when travel crosses stitches already sewn. Menu bar (File, Edit, Object, Type, View, Window, Help) with the usual ⌘ shortcuts. Help › Report an Issue… opens a new issue on GitHub in your browser, started with which ZigZag you have and what it's running on. It's the real macOS menu bar on a Mac, drawn in the window elsewhere. Crash logs: if something inside ZigZag fails badly enough to stop it, a short log of what failed and where is kept in the settings folder ( crashes/ , the newest ten; Help › Show Crash Logs opens it). The next time ZigZag opens it offers to report it: a GitHub issue started with the gist of the log, and the file shown so it can be attached. Nothing is sent unless you post it, and people's names are taken out of the paths in it. Help also has ZigZag on GitHub, and About ZigZag links there too. Cursors drawn for each tool: the Pen's nib (with what a click will do), crosshairs for the Shape, Measure and Fill Angle tools, Direct Selection's hollow arrow, and a curved arrow at rotate corners. Right-click menus on the canvas and the Layers list, styled like the tool flyouts: the stitch types with their icons, then the usual commands with their shortcuts. Stays quick on big designs: stitches are planned once per change, reusing every object that didn't change (overlap removal too: moving one object redoes only the objects it overlaps); a design that takes more than 12 ms to plan plans in the background (the status bar says "Updating stitches…" and the last plan stays on screen meanwhile; when you drop a moved object its stitches move with it until the new plan lands). Dragging points or objects, and typing, preview without re-planning until you let go. The stitches live on the GPU: each color block's segments are uploaded once and drawn by a shader (thread shading and needle points included), so panning, zooming, dragging and the stitch player cost nothing per stitch on the CPU, whether the design has a thousand stitches or half a million. The Layers list lays out only the rows in view. An object whose stitches hit an internal error is left out with a warning in Issues rather than taking the plan down. For development: TL_PROFILE=1 prints each frame's sections to stderr, TL_NO_GPU=1 draws the stitches with the painter instead, and cargo test --release --features gui --bin zigzag-studio perf_bench -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 times typing and dragging on a traced logo ( examples/bench-grid.svg is a 213,000-stitch design for the studio itself). Follows the system's light or dark appearance ( ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark overrides) and uses the San Francisco system font on a Mac. Pick a stitch type per object: big buttons, the task bar, right-click, or F/S/R/C/X (Blanket and Manual from the Stitch panel). The preview re-plans live. Layout, the Illustrator way: drag to move (Shift: 45° steps; Option: drag a copy). Handles resize freely (Shift keeps proportions, Option resizes from the center, drag past the far side to flip); just outside a corner rotates (Shift: 45°). Smart guides snap edges and centers to other objects and the hoop (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U). ⌘D is Transform Again: Option-drag a copy, then ⌘D for more at the same spacing. Hold Space to pan with any tool (a tap plays the stitch-out). The Transform panel has Illustrator's reference point: X/Y show the chosen point and W/H resize around it. Also rotate, flip, center in hoop, fit to hoop (artwork bigger than the hoop is scaled down to fit when you open or place it; Undo restores full size), ⌘C/⌘V, arrows nudge 0.5 mm (Shift 5 mm). Edits are saved as SVG transforms. Groups work like Illustrator: a click or drag takes the whole group; double-click goes into it (the rest dims and a breadcrumb shows where you are), double-click again to go deeper; Esc or double-click on empty canvas comes back out. ⌘-click picks one object without going in. Layers (Illustrator's "Layer 1", Inkscape layers, Figma frames) aren't groups. Copy, paste and duplicate keep groups. Type (T), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: click where the text should go and type straight onto the canvas (Enter for a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere when done); click text, or between its letters, to edit it with the caret where you clicked (or double-click it with the Selection tool, which picks text anywhere in its box and shows it as a box, not its letters' points; delete every letter and finish, and the text is removed) (←/→, ↑/↓, Home/End and ⌘←/→ move it; Backspace and Delete remove either side; Shift with any of those, a drag, a double-click for a word, a triple-click or ⌘A for the lot selects text, which typing replaces and ⌘C/⌘X/⌘V copy, cut and paste); click a selected path to put text on it. The Lettering panel is a compact Character panel (hat text isn't long copy): font (with search), bold/italic, letter height, tracking, pair kerning (pick the pair, or Option+←/→ while typing kerns the pair at the caret), horizontal and vertical scale, case (as typed, UPPER, lower, Title), alignment and leading for two-line text, baseline (straight, arc over, arc under, or on a path with offset and flip), and the stitch type. The Type menu has Type on a Path, Change Case, Align and Create Outlines (⇧⌘O). Text is a shape like any other: Direct Selection, Round Corners, Simplify, Pathfinder and Clean Up all work on it (it quietly becomes plain paths at the first point-level edit, one undo step), and it saves as real SVG text until then. Pen (P): draw filled shapes or lines with corners and curves, or place manual stitches one by one. Snaps to the grid when it's showing, else to smart guides. Shapes (M, L, \): rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, polygons, stars and lines. Measure , mm grid , needle points , First/Last , Group colors . Open machine files (PES, PEC, DST, EXP, JEF) to view, resize and re-export them, and images to trace. Settings per type: fill angle (with a drag-to-set angle tool , A ), spacing, length, pull, underlay. Satin options: column vs border, stitch (satin, S-stitch, zig-zag), threads across the column, width, underlay passes, short stitches. Contour and ripple: rings or spiral. Cross-stitch: cell size. Tartan: the stripes (color and width each, mirrored), angle, row spacing. Run options: single or triple. Lean in the Stitch panel, for satins: how far the stitches lean from square across the column (a few degrees keeps them from sinking between a knit's rows; more shows a slant, like a leaf's veins). Sewing row in the Stitch panel: Start and End (click the outline; green and red markers you can drag), Trim and Stop after the object. Edit › Copy / Paste Stitch Settings carries one object's type and settings to others (each keeps its thread and start/end); Edit › Select Same Stitch Type; Object › Path › Reverse Direction sews a path from its other end. Test swatches (Object › Test Swatches…): copies of the selection in a grid, one setting (spacing, length, pull compensation, satin width, fill angle) stepped from a value to another, each lettered with its value, to stitch out and compare on the real fabric. View › Density Map tints where stitches pile up (yellow from 2.5 per mm², red at 4), and View › Sewing Order numbers the objects on the canvas. Machine in the Document panel: choose the machine a design is for (Brother's 4×4, 5×7 and PR machines, the Skitch, Janome's 550E, Husqvarna Viking's Jade 35, Melco's Summit, ZSK's Sprint 8, any commercial machine that reads DST, or one of your own) and its hoops lead the Hoop menu, Export offers the file it reads first, and new documents start set up for it. What the machine asks of the stitches (a shortest stitch, its own locks) shows under the row. The gear beside it, and Machine Settings… in the menu, open Settings. A machine is a name for ordinary settings, saved into the design, so a file opens the same anywhere. Settings (ZigZag › Settings…, ⌘, ; at the foot of Edit on Windows and Linux): what's set once for this computer. Machines: ZigZag's and yours; + makes one from the document's hoop, Duplicate copies one (ZigZag's own can't be changed, but a copy can); each has its name, hoops (and the one new documents start in), the file it reads, a shortest stitch for machines that drop short ones, and its lock stitches (back and forth, a triangle or none, with their length and number). With a shortest stitch, nothing in the plan or the file is shorter: fill rows closer together than that are sewn every second row and then the rows between (the same needle points, longer turns), other short stitches are merged into their neighbours, and locks are never shorter than it. General: units, light or dark, and whether stitches are drawn on the GPU. Agent: which agent the Agent panel runs, and the server other agents connect to (on or off, and its port; from the next launch). Narrow satin in the Document panel: satins narrower than this (1 mm unless you say) get the too-narrow warning. Set it to what sews cleanly on your fabric. Fabric preset, hoop, Remove overlaps and Cap order in the Document panel. The hoop menu has the standard sizes from 1×2.5 in (20 × 60 mm) to 9.5×14 in (240 × 360 mm), the Skitch's two and Janome's A and B; Custom takes any width and height, for magnetic and other frames. Preview on your hat's color. Issues list (status bar): problems link to the object. Satins show their rails on the canvas. Sewing order: Earlier/Later. Stitch player (Space). Undo/redo everything. Save (Ctrl/⌘ S) writes settings into the SVG; Export PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC/PEN or a worksheet (HTML: picture, size, time, every color stop with the nearest Brother and Janome thread); Send to Skitch . Measuring and units. Measure (I) works like VectorCraft's: drag between two points to read the distance, angle, width and height. The ends snap to points, edges and the hoop (or to the grid when it's on), Shift keeps the line to 45°, and the reading stays until the next drag (Escape clears it). View › Units, or the unit menu in the status bar, shows sizes, positions, distances and the grid in millimeters, centimeters, inches, points or pixels (SVG pixels, 1/96 in, as files are read); it's remembered between launches. Any length field also takes a typed unit or a sum ( 1/4 in , 25.4mm , 10+5 ). The grid (⌘') follows the unit, inches in halves down to 1/32, and labels its major lines along the canvas's top and left edges from the hoop's center. Stitch settings (spacing, density, pull compensation) stay in millimeters. Picks up where you left off. Quit (or crash) and reopen: the same files come back, every tab with any unsaved changes, the zoom and the selection, and the same tab in front. Changes are kept as you work ( session.json and one recovery file per tab, recovery.svg , recovery-2.svg …, in ZigZag's settings folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/ZigZag ), each written whole or not at all), never written into your file until you save. Opening the app with a file skips this. If the app went down while bringing a document back, the next launch keeps it aside as recovery-crashed.svg instead of trying again (and an unreadable one as recovery-unreadable.svg ), and says so in the status bar. A job on the Skitch comes back too: the design last sent is kept ( sent.json ), the Skitch window reopens if it was open and reconnects, and once the machine reports that design its progress shows on it again (the machine keeps the design and where the needle is; Stop ends the job on both). Agents (MCP) The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step. MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp Claude Desktop / stdio clients ( claude_desktop_config.json ): { "mcpServers" : { "zigzag" : { "command" : " /path/to/zigzag-mcp " } } } zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching ( zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio ), kept only when the agent saves or exports it. Tools: get_design , add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object , delete_object , move_object transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects add_text , edit_text , list_fonts set_document (machine, shortest stitch, lock stitches, how narrow a satin may be before it's warned about, fabric, hoop as a standard or any WIDTHxHEIGHT in mm, overlaps, cap order, preview color), list_machines , group_colors render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design , get_svg , select export with objects: true also writes FILE.objects.json : which object each stitch, jump and trim in the machine file is for, so a checker can name the shape behind a fault open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents , switch_document , new_document , undo , save , export (machine formats or html worksheet; without a format, the one the path ends in, or else the one the document's machine reads), send_to_skitch , machine_status Any tool that changes the design takes terse: true for a short answer (ok, the names of objects added, and the design problems that are new) instead of the whole object; on batch it covers every step. trace_image (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF logo → shapes, colors snapped to a thread chart), add_outline (a satin or running-stitch outline on a filled shape, as an object of its own), round_corners , simplify (VectorCraft's 0–100 levels, or Auto), clean_up , simplify_design (fewer threads, small details and trims for the whole design; dry_run to see what it comes to) batch : several calls in one, all or nothing and one undo step; later steps can use earlier results ( "$0.added.0.name" ) Arguments a tool doesn't take are refused with the ones it does (a misspelt widht_mm isn't silently ignored), and each tool says whether it only reads. Try asking: "Draw a 50 mm round badge with mountains and a sun for my thin cotton cap, check it, and show me the preview." CLI zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o logo.jef -o preview.png -o sheet.html [--fabric thin-cap] [--hat] zigzag convert old.dst -o old.pes # machine files convert too zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes # PNG, JPEG, WebP… logos are traced first zigzag info logo.svg # stats + checks zigzag fabrics # list presets zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --machine melco-summit # that machine's hoop and shortest stitch zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.dst --min-stitch 0.4 --lock triangle:0.5:3 zigzag machines # list machines zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --objects # and logo.exp.objects.json: which object each stitch is for zigzag skitch info | status # needs --features ble zigzag skitch send logo.svg --trace Illustrator workflow Export with File → Export → Export As → SVG (Styling: Presentation Attributes, Object IDs: Layer Names). Outline text, or it falls back to system fonts. Opening the ZigZag-saved SVG back in Illustrator keeps the settings in the layer names. Name layers or objects to set their stitching. Illustrator's _x3D_ -style escapes are decoded, and group settings apply to everything inside the group. Token Meaning fill satin run skip stitch type a=45 fill angle (degrees) s=0.3 row / zigzag spacing (mm) l=3 max stitch length (mm) pc=0.2 pull compensation (mm per side) w=3 satin width (mm) border satin along a filled shape's outline instead of across it u=0 underlay off ul=center+contour+zigzag satin underlay passes ( ul=none ) ss=0 short stitches off r=3 running passes (3 = bean) contour blanket applique manual the other stitch types split=7 satin auto-split length (mm); split=0 off t=e8a33c thread color override o=2 sewing order stroke.… applies only to the stroke of an object that also has a fill, e.g. stroke.run (the object's other settings are its fill's) Example layer names: logo fill a=45 s=0.35 , title satin , outline stroke.satin stroke.w=1.5 . Skitch over Bluetooth The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done). Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time. Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done. Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered ; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design. Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop. Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too. Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume. Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does). Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end. The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning). The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine , which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch. Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status . The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates. Working out undocumented commands Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do: Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log . zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] ( --all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both: iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode ) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace ( .pklg ). Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it. Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same. Ink/Stitch parity Checked against Ink/Stitch 's features and tool docs: Ink/Stitch ZigZag Running, bean, manual stitch; satin column (two rails with rungs), E-stitch; tatami, contour, circular (spiral) fill ✓ Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓ Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row) Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline, under what's sewn on top), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect bar) Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓ Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts) Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓ Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓ Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet Hatch parity Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set: Hatch ZigZag Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓ Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓ Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets) Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts) Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓ Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool) Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓ Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓ Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only) Production worksheet ✓ (HTML) Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines) Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet Status Verified: 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace. Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files. PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences. Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP. Tested on a real Brother Skitch (PP1). Screenshots and videos Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg). Credits See NOTICE , and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md for the licenses of the libraries ZigZag is built from (regenerate it with packaging/licenses/generate.sh after changing dependencies). PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). Image Trace is vendored from VectorCraft (MIT OR Apache-2.0), whose curve fitting, live corners, snap targets and colour difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md ). Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch . About Free, open-source embroidery software for Mac and Windows. Turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and create designs with AI agents via MCP. zigzag.diy/ Topics brother-skitch embroidery embroidery-digitizing embroidery-software machine-embroidery macos mcp model-context-protocol rust svg vector-editor windows Resources Readme Apache-2.0 license Activity Stars 737 stars Watchers 6 watching Forks 37 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. title: All US airports are currently ground stopped
