title: Tim Peters has died
body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 232 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 12 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 19 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 51 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered. Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim. He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so. Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start. Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim. When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . C 44 Likes duncathan (Dunc Graham) November 11, 2026, 6:46am 6 As a young child, only about 15, I first learned timsort. Some dozen years later, I had the briefest opportunity to exchange words with Tim himself on this forum. What a treat to have had that chance, just in time. RIP 12 Likes encukou (Petr Viktorin) November 11, 2026, 8:32am 7 When I was finishing university, head full of textbook algorithms, I read Objects/listsort.txt and was overwhelmed by how much depth, rigor, common sense and humanity can fit in a technical note. That was when I picked a programming language. 33 Likes pitrou (Antoine Pitrou) November 11, 2026, 9:53am 8 Tim’s main legacy for me has been the Zen of Python, which - despite being less cited nowadays - has been so useful and influential as a framework for elegance and clarity, and has informed so many people in their daily practice (and I cannot find a better way to describe him than as an excellent practitioner ). He was already less active when I started contributing around 2007; in fact my most frequent interactions with him have been in the recent years while he grew a slightly more confrontational attitude in some discussions, including here on d.p.o. I believe [1] he was acting with the best of intentions and was still deeply caring for the community he had been such a pivotal member of; acting with the same objectives as others, but having trouble to understand that different means might be used towards the same ends. and I might be full of myself here ↩︎ 19 Likes malemburg (Marc-André Lemburg) November 11, 2026, 9:58am 9 This is so sad and such a big loss for Python. Tim has given us a lot and we owe him. He was one of the extremely smart people who drew me into PythonLand in the late 1990s. Coming out of university, I was amazed how approachable, down to earth and humurous really great folks can be. Rest in Peace, Tim, and thanks-for-being-one-of-those-great-people-ly, Marc 22 Likes pf_moore (Paul Moore) November 11, 2026, 10:51am 10 So sad. I never had the chance to meet Tim in person, but his posts were always a delight to read, full of knowledge, insight and humour. I learned more than I can express from him. He will be missed. 15 Likes hodgestar (Simon Cross) November 11, 2026, 10:55am 11 One of the great souls, and roughly treated here near the end. 15 Likes nas (Neil Schemenauer) November 11, 2026, 12:31pm 12 A +1 to what Chris wrote. Tim was always pragmatic, preferring simple solutions over complex ones. In the early days of syntax highlighting in text editors, like Emacs and Vim, I remember that Python’s triple-quoted strings were tricky to get right. They span multiple lines and opening and closing tokens are identical, so it’s easy to get out of sync. Doctests make things especially tricky. I was telling Tim about some techniques I was using in the Vim syntax file to make it work more reliably. I don’t recall the editor Tim used (some commercial program on Windows) but he explained how he did it in his editor. Open the syntax highlighting config window, for open string token, type three quotes, for close string, type three quotes, close config window. Job done. That tickled him. He primarily used Windows 95 or 98 at a time when many Python core devs used NT, Unix, or Linux. He said if you installed all of Microsoft’s updates, it was quite reliable. Maybe he preferred it because it worked for him and there was no reason to change. Or, he found it useful when supporting people, since Windows was the most common platform Python was used on. Tim was about the furthest thing from an elitist you could be. This Bible quote comes to mind for me: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.”. Tim gave us a lot of fruit. I poked around at Python 2.4, since that seems a good version to show off the things he worked on. His contributions were all over the codebase but I’ll point out a few that stand out to me. pymalloc was contributed by Vladimir Marangozov but it was Tim who polished it to diamond-like form. A memory allocator is one of those things where it is impossible to have something completely optimal; you always make tradeoffs. Tim’s special contribution in that unit is Py_ADDRESS_IN_RANGE . It is well commented, if you want to understand how it works. Technically, it relies on undefined behavior but Tim figured it should work in practice. It did so for many years. At some point I wanted to increase the pymalloc pool size, since typical RAM sizes had increased so much since 2000. Tim helped me optimize the address_in_range() check. TimSort is a good example of Tim’s approach to software problems. Someone must have “nerd sniped” him on the problem of sorting. He already had an encyclopedic knowledge of the classic algorithms, like you’d find in Knuth. He spent a few days reading the recent research papers on sorting. With that knowledge and throwing in a few twists of his own, he made TimSort. He was always thinking of the common case, the favorable case as well as the worst-case scenarios. TimSort does all three well (it exploits already sorted runs, and uses galloping during merging to copy long stretches efficiently). Speaking of Knuth, the dict object algorithms were heavily optimized by Tim. The C file contains lots of comments. He also wrote dictnotes , which is a good example of his technical writing. Another example is weakref.txt , which I think Tim wrote after fixing a particularly difficult GC bug revealed by ZODB (while working at Zope Corp). On the topic of GC, the initial version of the cyclic garbage collector was written by me, merged before the 2.0 release. It was Tim who polished it into robust and well-performing shape. Likewise, I wrote the initial version of “simple generators” but it was Tim who put them on solid foundation, both the PEP and the implementation. Tim was skilled with numerical algorithms and error analysis, and Python benefited from his expertise. The float object and math module got special attention from him. He also worked on the Karatsuba multiplication algorithms in longobject . In addition to the C code, Tim also wrote beautiful Python code. As an example, see the N-Queens and Knight’s tour solvers in test_generators.py . He wrote the initial version of doctest . Some more examples of his work: difflib , pickletools , tabnanny (she shows no mercy!). It’s clear that Tim enjoyed writing code and solving problems. It’s also the case that he spent many thousands of hours of his time doing things primarily to help his fellow humans, without expectation of financial gain or of glory. Thank you, friend, for that and thank you for setting such an example. 46 Likes vinitkme (Vinit Kumar) November 11, 2026, 12:58pm 13 Thanks for everything Tim. Zen of Python has always been and will be my programming " North Star" and I strive to use it in every language I work with. Your impact has been on many of us Python Programmers and our families lives. Thank you and rest in peace! 9 Likes Stefan2 (Stefan Pochmann) November 11, 2026, 1:09pm 14 I’ve been fearing this since I noticed his absence end of July, dreading the thought whenever I saw his name but still no new activity. I’ve had quite a few interactions with Tim, he was one of my main contact points to Python, and he was the one who added me to Misc/ACKS . Thank you for everything, Tim. 8 Likes Paddy3118 (Paddy3118) November 11, 2026, 1:30pm 16 GNU Tim. 5 Likes diegor (Diego Russo) November 11, 2026, 2:39pm 17 I wish I’d had the chance to meet Tim in person. We had just a few exchanges on social media, but I always enjoyed reading his messages. There was always something to learn from his experience, his perspective and his way of thinking. Reading the memories shared here by those who knew and worked with him makes me regret even more that I never had that opportunity. I remember when Timsort was created. I was at university, studying algorithms, and it was a big deal at the time. But it’s the Zen of Python that influenced me most personally. “Now is better than never.” That sentence has stayed with me since I started using Python in the early 2000s. Over the years, it has become one of my personal mottos, encouraging me to keep trying, strive to do better and step outside my comfort zone, both in life and at work. We’ll probably never know what the 20th aphorism of the Zen of Python would have been. But perhaps that’s OK. I like to think that Tim left us the freedom to fill that space with something meaningful to each of us. Thank you, Tim, for everything you gave to Python and for the impact your work and words had on people. Rest in peace. 15 Likes holdenweb (Steve Holden) November 11, 2026, 3:09pm 18 Tim and I originally thought we first met fairly shortly after we both moved to Virginia, and became friends over Chinese lunches and discussions with Guido about starting a new Python conference. As we got to know each other better we realised that we had seen each other once before, when I visited a fellow academic’s office in Manchester, England, and Tim was there representing Cray Research back in 1983. Small world. After PythonLabs dissolved on Guido’s departure for the West coast the lunches eventually became a regular date at our local PF Chang, where Tim would invariably end with their huge “Mountain of Chocolate” dessert. The resulting sugar rush was often amusing. Tim was well-known long before I arrived in the Python world, and remained so after I left it. His technical contributions to Python, now the most popular programming language in the world, are legion. Just as significant, if not more so, was the way he communicated the joy, both of being a programmer and a human being. He was deeply affected by the ban imposed on him for ideological reasons by the Python Steering Committee but did not let that affect his desire to help others, which was on display until the end. I respected Tim above anyone else in the Python world for his wisdom, his witty humour and his deep humanity. There won’t be another one like him. Goodbye, old friend. 28 Likes sdeibel (Stephan Deibel) November 11, 2026, 3:41pm 19 This is very sad. I worked with Tim for quite a few years in context of the PSF board and of course also knew him from IPC and PyCons, starting in the relatively early days. He stood out to me almost immediately because so obviously utterly brilliant and yet with such a kind, helpful, respectful, good-humored way about him. One of the best people I’ve known, he was an inspiration to me and I think clearly also to very many others. Thanks, Tim, you will be missed. 13 Likes mwichmann (Mats Wichmann) November 11, 2026, 3:42pm 20 I only met Tim once, along with Guido, in 2001. I was writing a Python training course, and the training company wanted to arrange for “the experts” to get a look at it, so on a week I was in Reston working on it, we sat down over a meal. It wasn’t a very good course (“if I knew then what I know now”, a quarter century later…), but they generously gave of their time to critique, including Tim’s trademark humor, and I so appreciated it. He will be missed! 8 Likes mdickinson (Mark Dickinson) November 11, 2026, 4:00pm 22 Tim was hugely influential on my own CPython core development journey. Initially that influence was through his voluminous writings, mailing list discussions and his code itself: when I joined the core dev team in 2008, Tim himself was absent from the scene in person, but very much present through his many many contributions. Later on, after his return to core development, I was privileged to interact more directly with Tim on many topics. His gentle erudition, his humour and his patience were endless. Rest in peace, Tim. You will be sorely missed. 18 Likes next page → Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

Â· 3 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Share Today, weâre rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency. Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static âmodel routerâ that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks. Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation. Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argonâs 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flashâs 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier. Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text. Getting started Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business . title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
body_text: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac Skip to main content Toggle main menu 9to5Mac Logo Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site 9to5Toys 9to5Google Logo 9to5Google Electrek Drone DJ Logo DroneDJ Space Explored About Privacy Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Search for: Submit Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts Apple@Work Happy Hour 9to5Mac Daily Overtime iPhone iPhone Mac Mac MacBook Pro MacBook Air iMac Mac mini Mac Studio Mac Pro iPad iPad Pro iPad Air iPad mini iPad iPadOS Watch Apple Watch Apple Watch Ultra Apple Health Apple Watch SE Vision Vision Pro visionOS Music and TV Apple Music AirPods HomePod Apple TV Guides Reviews How Tos AAPL Apple Store Apple Arcade Apple Card Apple Silicon Apple One Apple Fitness+ CarPlay Siri HomeKit Toggle dark mode AI Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy Ryan Christoffel  | Nov 10 2026 - 11:15 am PT 0 Comments Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Gemini 4 Hydrogen is available Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads Scaling developer and enterprise workflows Adaptable speed and intelligence across thinking levels Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search Designed for safe, dependable execution for scale Available to everyone today Last updated November 13, 2026 Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows. While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity . Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs. Scaling developer and enterprise workflows Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows: Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash. Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena , arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA . Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. Web development : On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts. Using Hydrogen for on-the-fly 3D coding, Geminisland lets anyone add to a shared voxel island from a single prompt to generate custom structures live on the map that players can walk around and explore in first person. Try the live app . Paired with our new Gemini front end design skill in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen built an e-commerce storefront in one shot complete with a WebGL2 topographic shader, pinned four-stage scrollytelling, a thermal split-slider, a 3D wireframe spec card, and a live finish configurator. Try the live app and the Gemini front end design skill . In Google Antigravity, Hydrogen turned Google Sheets into an animated pixel canvas by shrinking thousands of cells combining Python, native =LET(...) formulas, and conditional formatting to paint and animate full-motion scenes directly inside a live spreadsheet. Starting from a YouTube keynote video and a design template in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen generated a multi-slide presentation directly in Google Slides, then ran an autonomous audit-and-fix loop to catch overlapping text and clean up every slide layout. With Gemini in Google Sheets, Hydrogen can help teams rapidly turn financial data into interactive models that dynamically adjust based on various forecasting scenarios, generating outputs over 30% faster than previous models in Sheets canvas. Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens. Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations. In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth. Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details. Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list. Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe. Moving fast from idea to working prototype, Hydrogen built an interactive 3D globe and Web Audio music engine driven by real-time lightning strikes and mapped every bolt around the world into visual ripples and live ambient music. When tasked to create a WebGL2 water and glass visualizer, Hydrogen built it from pure math and SDF textures — simulating real-time light refraction, reflection, dispersion, and absorption. Using a custom skill for video assembly and adhering to a creative brief, Gemini 4 Hydrogen created an archival sizzle reel about the element ‘Hydrogen’, sourcing public-domain footage and cutting it into one continuous edit with clean narration. Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search , delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally. Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for. More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search. Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered. Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work: Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 94% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation. Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency , Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%. For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card . Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces: For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio , try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity . For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol
body_text: The Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol | Brave Yes Dismiss Browser Downloads Desktop Android iOS Features Shields adblocker VPN Privacy features Premium services Brave Origin Browser AI More features Brave vs. other browsers Search Try Brave Search Ask Brave Search features Web Discovery Project Brave vs. other search engines Search API Get started Get API key API features Use cases Sign up Log in Resources Developer docs How-to guides Tools & integrations MCP Server Latest API news Brave Ads Overview Browser Ads Search Ads Resources Help center Ads manager Get Brave Search the Web a]:no-underline [&>a]:text-text-primary"> All blog posts AI news & features B2B & advertiser news BAT, creators, & Brave Rewards Brave Search news Browser performance Company news Developers & community New products & features Policy & legislation Privacy updates Research Web3, crypto, & NFTs WebStandards@Brave All topics AI news & features B2B & advertiser news BAT, creators, & Brave Rewards Brave Search news Browser performance Company news Developers & community New products & features Policy & legislation Privacy updates Research Web3, crypto, & NFTs WebStandards@Brave Blog > Brave Search news The Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol Published Nov 12, 2026 Share on X (formerly Twitter) Share on Reddit Share on Telegram Share on LinkedIn Brave Search news The Brave Search API , our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management. Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine. How does it work? Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain. Get started today Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service. The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today. Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Our answer is a URL cloaking scheme built on partially oblivious pseudorandom functions, so bots get more expensive and we still never learn which result you clicked. title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
body_text: Jane Street Blog - Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Home All Posts Machine Learning Authors Index Jane Street Subscribe to email updates Subscribe to Email Updates Featured Reads Read more Using ASCII waveforms to test hardware designs Read more Finding memory leaks with Memtrace Tags async book c camlp4 code-review comments compiler core hackerschool hg incremental internship interviewing machine-learning ocaml parallel-programming performance ppx real-world-ocaml registers speed ui Get the RSS feed Jane Street Open Source Join Our Team Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Nov 02, 2026 | 3 min read Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn By: Matthew Saffer Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all. We’ve talked about this recently in a podcast on how we use AI in our development , and in a post on formal methods that touches on how agentic coding is reshaping the way we work. Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go. That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things. So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance. We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months. A few things worth knowing: Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect. The rest of our process is unchanged. If you’ve read our earlier posts about interviewing here , they’re still accurate. While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that. Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else. As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work. As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say. If you’re interested in working with us, apply on our website ! title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
body_text: Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System The dwarf planet candidate, called ED138, appeared in telescope images and takes roughly 280 years to orbit the sun. Astronomers need to determine its size to properly classify it Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science November 12, 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source The new dwarf planet candidate, called 2026 ED138, orbits on a plane tiled nearly 25 degrees compared to our solar system's main planets, suggesting it was disturbed by gravitational interactions with Neptune. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor Image Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Orbit data provided by the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPCorb catalog), funded by NASA PDCO and the Tamkin Foundation. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big. Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.” Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became. “We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says. The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system. “This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.” 2026 ED138 3D orbit Watch on Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.) Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions. ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger. Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says. Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light. Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.” The Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in these images between March and June this year. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA Image Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto , Eris , Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.” The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds. What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert. “Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement . “I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb , a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN ’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.” Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood. “Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.” You Might Also Like Astronomers Discover a Possible Dwarf Planet Far Beyond Neptune, Where There Should Have Only Been Empty Space May 29, 2025 Meet Farout, the Solar System's Most Distant Minor Planet December 18, 2018 Astronomers Discover 'Ammonite,' a Mysterious Distant Object That Could Shed Light on Our Solar System's History July 22, 2025 Say Hello to Our Solar System’s Newest Dwarf Planet October 13, 2016 Astronomers Propose New Criteria to Classify Planets, but Pluto Still Doesn't Make the Cut July 19, 2024 Carlyn Kranking is Smithsonian magazine's associate web editor for science. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead. AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator . Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide Quick start With an AI coding agent Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent . aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Server mode (CLI and any SDK) Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux . Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker . Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator . Embedded mode (Rust tests) Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost. Known issues To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator . Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ . Building from source You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above. Prerequisites A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. Build and run cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate). Embedded mode build cost Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change. Repository layout . ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues Telemetry AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties. For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator . To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options. Use a command-line option Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t ) set to off . This setting applies only to that emulator process. aws-emulator --telemetry off In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command. Use an environment variable Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell. EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on , true , or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off , false , or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning. export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator Use a configuration file To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml . The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path. [ telemetry ] enabled = false Use the embedded configuration API In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator. use aws_emulator_embedded :: { AwsEmulatorEmbedded , EmbeddedOptions , Telemetry } ; fn main ( ) { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded :: new ( EmbeddedOptions :: default ( ) . telemetry ( Telemetry :: Off ) ) ; let _http_client = emulator . http_client ( ) ; } You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off. Reporting issues and contributing Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues . The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs. TV boxes, old phones and tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself. Three devices so far 📺 Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) 📱 iPad Air (2013) 📲 OnePlus Nord CE 2 (2022) Chip Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 Apple A7, 2 cores MediaTek Dimensity 900, 2× Cortex-A78 + 6× A55 RAM 1.9 GB (about 1 GB usable) 1 GB (about 700 MB usable) 7.4 GB (about 3 GB free) OS Android 14, no root iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken Android 13, no root Everyday model Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 4.9-5.7 tok/s Biggest model Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 5.1 tok/s Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 2.6-4.5 tok/s Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B at 2.6-3.1 tok/s Full results docs/tv-box.md ipad-air/README.md docs/phone.md The TV box and the iPad run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM, and the phone runs 35B and 80B ones with about 3 GB free. They all keep only part of each model in memory and read the rest from flash as it's needed. The chart below compares the two 1 GB devices size class by size class; the phone plays in a bigger league, and its results are in docs/phone.md . More devices (single-board computers, routers, more phones) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM. Got a small device? Run a model on it and submit your numbers : we'll add them to the results. How it works All of it is a patch on llama.cpp . The main ideas: Kernels built for the chip. A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions. Less RAM per model. Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Experts paged from flash. A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB, and 35B and 80B models on a phone. Streaming for dense models bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed. docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its measured gain. Try it The quickest start is a ready-made model file from Hugging Face. The TV box and iPad files need the patched llama.cpp (stock llama.cpp can't load their pruned heads); the phone files load anywhere, but their speeds need the patch's expert pager. TV box or another ARMv8.2 Android device: docs/tv-box-setup.md Jailbroken iPad on iOS 12: ipad-air/README.md Android phone with 8 GB of RAM: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (12.3 GB) and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (27.6 GB, two files), set up as in docs/phone.md . title: IceWM
body_text: IceWM | Window Manager IceWM Window Manager IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs. Software IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github . Releases The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06). Features Easy to use, simple and fast Standards compliant → Fully usable with keyboard Alt+Tab window switching Efficient resource usage Task bar (optional) Multiple workspaces Fully documented → A large number of themes → Usable with GNOME and KDE environments Regenerates menus when configuration changes Support for sound effects → Multiple focus modes Manual placement of windows option Autoraising of windows option Tooltips Configurable keybindings → Supports DockApps in a container Tabbed windows Screenshots The IceWM Screenshots Collection Themes IceWM is themeable . The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme, which is a collection of settings and small images. Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org . Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list . Translations IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there , then update . Documentation IceWM man pages IceWM Manual Themes Howto IceWM FAQ Bug Tracking Report your icewm bugs on Github . Only report it once and give relevant details. Install the latest release as follows $ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz $ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz $ cd icewm-4.1.0 $ ./configure --prefix = /usr $ make $ sudo make install Install from unreleased development source code Gettext must be installed. $ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm $ cd icewm $ ./autogen.sh $ ./configure --prefix = /usr $ make $ sudo make install If you have cmake, an alternative is: $ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm $ cd icewm $ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix = /usr $ cd build $ sudo make install Install package dependencies To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script. $ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh $ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh Verify package dependencies by: $ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg # or simpler: $ ./rebuild.sh -d More installation and configuration IceWM from scratch . Trigger phrases: 'teach me', 'tutor me', 'quiz me', 'drill me', 'help me master'. Not for one-off 'explain X' or 'what is X' questions. Socratic Tutor Act as a personal tutor that takes the user from their current level to genuine mastery of a topic using the maieutic (Socratic) method: teach primarily by asking questions that force the user to reason, predict, and explain — not by lecturing. Guard: confirm intent before starting This skill is for an ongoing teaching session, not for answering questions. If the user asked a one-off question ("explain X", "what is X", "how do I use X"), answer it normally and do not start the tutoring loop. If intent is ambiguous, ask one short question ("Want a quick answer, or should I actually teach you this properly?") before launching the diagnostic. A false start costs the user an unwanted quiz; a confirmation costs one word. Session start Break the topic into 4-10 concrete subskills (fewer for narrow topics). For broad topics, make a two-level tree and pick the first branch to work on. Tell the user that you will start by asking a few questions, one at a time, to see what they already know. Run a short diagnostic: 3-5 probing questions spanning easy to hard, to place the user's starting level per subskill. Do not teach anything until the diagnostic is done. Show the initial skill map (format below) and propose where to start. Let the user override. Skill map Track each subskill at levels 0-5: 0 unaware . 1 heard of it . 2 can follow along . 3 can do with help 4 can do independently . 5 can teach it / handle edge cases Render the map as ASCII after every level change, and whenever the user asks for progress: Topic: <topic> overall: ######.... 58% ----------------------------------------------------------------- subskill A [########..] 4/5 * independent subskill B [######....] 3/5 <- current focus subskill C [##........] 1/5 ----------------------------------------------------------------- Use solid/light block characters (U+2588 / U+2591) for the bars when rendering. Teaching loop (repeat per subskill) Ask ONE question at a time. End the message immediately after the question and wait for the answer; do not add hints, example answers, or teaching content after it. Prefer questions that make the user: predict an outcome, explain why, find the flaw in a plausible-but-wrong claim, apply an idea to a new case, or connect two ideas. When the user is wrong, do not give the answer. Ask a narrower question that exposes the contradiction in their reasoning. Only explain directly after 2-3 failed attempts, and then immediately re-test the same idea from a different angle. When the user is right, occasionally play devil's advocate ("are you sure? what about X?") — they should be able to defend correct answers under pressure. Give short explanations (a few sentences) only to introduce genuinely new material the user could not derive, then return to questioning. Where tools are available and relevant, set practical exercises (e.g. "write a query that...", "predict what this code prints") and check the user's actual output rather than their description of it. Evaluation rules — be strict Levels are earned, not given. Raise a level only on demonstrated performance across 2+ independent checks, at least one of them unprompted recall (not immediately after the user was told the answer). A vague or partially-correct answer is not correct. Probe until you know whether the user actually understands. Do not attribute to the user any insight they did not actually express. Interleave spaced review: periodically re-test earlier subskills without warning. If the user fails a review, lower the level and revisit. Level 5 requires the user to handle an edge case or adversarial question AND explain the concept clearly enough that you would trust them to teach it. Do not flatter. "Not quite — why would X happen if Y were true?" beats "Great try!". Mastery and completion The course ends only when every subskill is at the target level (default 4/5; 5/5 if the user asked for full mastery). Then run a final mixed assessment covering everything, with at least one question per subskill and one integrative problem. If the user passes, show the final map and a summary of their weakest areas. If not, back to the loop. Commands the user can use anytime "show progress" — render the skill map "harder" / "easier" — adjust difficulty "just tell me" — override Socratic mode for the current question only "save state" — emit a compact block (topic, skill map with levels, notes on misconceptions and what has been covered) that can be pasted into a new session to resume "resume from:" — followed by a saved state block; restore it and continue where it left off Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc.
