title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
body_text: Edge0-145B: Open-Source On-Device AI with 145B Parameters - edge0 Models Docs Solutions Research Blog Company Connect Introducing Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer November 12, 2026 · 19 min read · Edge0 releases Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. This release addresses those constraints in four ways: The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads. Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory. Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available. Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability. Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud. Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling. Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step. Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model. Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand. Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate. Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing. Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency. What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work. Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following: Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1 , ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4. Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond , close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3. Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench , ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5. Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations. Model DeepSWE 1.1 Terminal-Bench 2.1 HLE GPQA-Diamond IFBench AA-LCR Edge0-145B 64.6 86.52 35.4 90.4 80.6 79.3 Edge0-120B 53.6 81.3 31.0 87.4 79.3 81.0 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 58.7 83.3 35.9 91.7 81.3 79.1 Qwen3.8-27B 42.2 73.0 30.8 89.2 79.5 82.0 DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 54.4 82.7 33.8 90.8 79.2 79.7 Flint 40B — 54.9 — — 89.2 — Muse Glimmer — 51.7 22.0 83.5 77.0 83.3 Gemma 4 — 43.4 22.7 85.7 76.0 62.0 Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) — 78.2 40.0 91.3 62.5 78.0 Scores are percentages; higher is better. A dash means no public score is available, rather than a score of zero. Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from Edge0's internal evaluations. Claude-Opus-4.6 has no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. For Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation; HLE, GPQA, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis. The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE . The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively. DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report. Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint Edge0-145B combines a 72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory . Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop. Model Mean across six benchmarks Memory footprint \(measured or estimated\) Edge0-145B 72.8 29GB Edge0-120B 68.9 29GB Qwen3.8-27B 66.1 Approximately 18GB* Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 71.7 Approximately 70GB* DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 70.1 Approximately 87GB* The means cover DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, HLE, GPQA-Diamond, IFBench, and AA-LCR. Edge0 memory figures are measured internal peaks. Asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment and remain to be measured. Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score. [Figure: Quality versus peak memory, with 48GB laptop and 64GB workstation capacities marked. Lower memory and higher scores are better; the chart's vertical axis does not start at zero.] Local agents that plan, code, run, and check their work A single natural-language request can start an entire local workflow. Edge0-145B breaks down the requirements, plans the steps, writes code, and calls tools to run it. When something fails, it debugs and repairs the code. It then takes screenshots to inspect the result and keeps iterating until the work is complete. These projects often take dozens of rounds of planning, execution, and review. Local inference means those additional conversations, code revisions, and visual analyses incur no corresponding cloud-model token or API charges. Code and data can stay on the computer, and core model capabilities work offline. Video production: generating Tesla's Roadster explainer within an hour Edge0-145B produced an explainer about how Roadster could fly, handling technical research, scriptwriting, asset generation, and editing. We asked it to make the principles understandable to a general audience. The model ran locally without cloud-model calls or cloud token consumption, avoiding network round trips for inference. The video was generated within an hour. Producing comparable work manually would have taken a director and scriptwriter, a 3D modeler, an editor, and a physics expert a month. An AI video workflow could previously cost more than hundreds of dollars; local inference eliminates the corresponding cloud-model token and API fees. 3D modeling: a Manhattan city scene in Blender Edge0-145B built a 3D scene of Manhattan within an hour. Working in Blender from text and reference images, it constructed the scene, adjusted materials and lighting, and iterated on the rendered output. The workflow brings visual inspection, code generation, and revision together inside Blender. The model works with objects, spatial relationships, and the creative goal, going beyond the pixels in a reference image. It inspects the result, writes code, and makes changes without handing those steps back to a person. The entire process stays local. Creating a Manhattan-scale city scene manually would typically cost approximately $12,000-18,000 and take at least a month. A leading cloud model would still incur more than $150 in cloud token charges. Edge0-145B completes the local inference without those cloud-model token fees. Game development: playable games and a medieval city Edge0-145B can create playable games locally. We also used its 3D modeling capabilities to build an original medieval capital for a fantasy RPG and render a 20-second fly-through at game-trailer quality. The model planned the city independently and built it from scratch in Blender: city walls, more than a thousand old-town homes, a plaza fountain, a Gothic twin-tower facade, a rib-vaulted nave, and stained-glass windows. The fixed camera path made errors visible. Geometry clipping, occlusion, or incorrect proportions would appear along the route, so the model inspected the renders and corrected its work as it built. The workflow ran entirely locally. A leading cloud model required hundreds of tool calls and hundreds of millions of tokens for a single completion, using the same prompt, reference images, and camera route. Edge0-145B delivered it on a laptop without cloud-model token or API fees for local inference. An art team would typically spend weeks and thousands of dollars producing a city scene to this standard. Hardware control: code that flies a real drone Edge0-145B wrote the program for a real drone from one instruction: “Write a drone program that navigates through obstacles and finds a red backpack.” It generated the flight-control and visual-recognition programs locally. The drone then took off indoors, navigated through a dense row of obstacle poles, searched autonomously, and located the red backpack beside a wall. The task required no human-written code and no cloud call. Hardware developers can describe the behavior they want and have the model turn it into a program for a real device, without moving repeatedly between an editor, documentation, and debugging tools. PCB design: from KiCad layout to an assembly animation Edge0-145B took a PCB design from component placement through an assembly visualization. We asked it to design a board for itself. It started from scratch in KiCad, placed components, routed a two-layer board, and imported the design into Unreal Engine 5. It then set up cameras and lighting and rendered an animation of PCB fabrication and assembly. A single computer delivered work that previously required a hardware engineer and a 3D designer to hand tasks back and forth over several days. Schematics and board layouts can stay on the team's own hardware, supporting trade-secret protection and data-handling requirements without uploading the designs to a cloud model. Why Edge0: A Full Stack for On-Device AI Useful on-device AI requires model development, inference engineering, and hardware adaptation to work together. Our progress rests on three capabilities: developing complementary models quickly, optimizing the full stack, and carrying lessons from each deployment into the next. Our September release of Edge0-35B showed what that approach could deliver on a phone. Its launch post passed 1.2 million views on its first day without paid promotion in overseas communities. Researchers and technical experts at OpenAI, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and other companies shared it, and the model reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's overall Trending chart. We released the model weights and unified inference framework together, giving companies and researchers a standard approach they could reproduce. The release helped move the discussion of on-device AI from a few billion parameters to the 35B tier. Four Model Families for On-Device AI Over the past year, we released 200 models across four families. Each handles a different part of the work, from listening and speaking to fast decisions, memory, and complex agent tasks. Model family Role Models and capabilities Edge0 Complex agent tasks and vibe coding 145B and 120B models for laptops; 35B and 8B models for phones. The laptop models support vibe coding, while the phone models support agent tasks. Audio8 Listening and speaking ASR-Infinite and 3B, 0.6B, and 0.1B ASR models for speech recognition; 0.6B and 0.1B TTS models for speech synthesis; and a 0.1B Chat model for end-to-end voice interaction. Decision0 Fast decisions 0.6B and 3B models covering text, speech, and vision, with multimodal decisions in approximately 40 milliseconds. Embedding0 Memory A 0.6B multimodal embedding model for text, speech, images, video, and files, supporting local long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation \(RAG\). The portfolio spans tens of millions to more than a hundred billion parameters. Both Edge0 and Audio8 have reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's Trending chart. Models and Inference Systems Designed Together We develop the model and the inference framework together, building hardware constraints into training and optimizing the engine for different chips. This connects model capability with the software and hardware needed to use it locally. That work requires expertise in model development, inference frameworks, and low-level hardware adaptation. The combination is difficult for a company focused only on model development to reproduce. Hardware Optimizations That Carry into Each Deployment Each deployment gives us reusable optimizations for the next chip, model, or product. This matters because on-device hardware is fragmented: NPU architectures differ, as does support for numerical formats such as INT4, INT8, and FP4. A general-purpose model cannot automatically make full use of every chip. We adapt to individual platforms. Our portfolio now covers 95% of mainstream chip platforms, including Qualcomm, BES, Rockchip, Allwinner, D-Robotics, and NVIDIA, across headphones, glasses, phones, PCs, and robots. This is portfolio-wide coverage; model requirements vary, and it does not mean every device can run Edge0-145B. That deployment work now spans more than 5 million production devices. Our open-source models passed 15 million downloads within three months. By October 2026, we had more than 110,000 customer organizations. The portfolio figures come from company papers and internal testing. They describe the broader Edge0 portfolio; the 145B performance results in this article apply specifically to Edge0-145B. For Edge0-145B, day-one support covers macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA platforms such as RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090. The release includes one-click deployment tools and hardware guides. The Future of On-Device AI and the Cloud More complex work can stay on the device as local models approach cloud-level capability. Privacy, cost control, and offline access have long favored local execution; the remaining question was whether an on-device model could do the work. Edge0-145B expands the range of tasks for which it can. Why More AI Work Can Stay Local Local execution addresses four practical obstacles to adopting cloud-only AI: Control cloud-model costs. Local inference adds no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees as usage grows. Keep sensitive data local. Code, documents, and business records can stay on the hardware, giving teams control over data handling. Sustain a responsive experience. Model and inference-engine design address response speed, power use, system responsiveness, and continuous operation together. Keep core capabilities available offline. Local tasks continue when connectivity drops; features that depend on online information or services still need a connection. From Cloud First to More Complex Work On-Device We see the division of work between devices and the cloud shifting through three stages. Before September 2026: cloud first, with on-device support. Apple Intelligence reflected this stage: it protected privacy, but handled a limited range of tasks locally while more demanding work relied on cloud capabilities. After Edge0-35B's September 10 release: everyday tasks locally, complex tasks in the cloud. Local models could take on frequent requests that needed immediate responses. For one leading headphone manufacturer, our hybrid solution now handles 92% of AI usage on-device and 8% in the cloud. Everyday conversation accounts for most use cases on consumer wearables. With Edge0-145B: toward on-device first, with cloud support. Vibe coding and other complex tasks can now run on a personal computer, giving teams more scope to choose local execution. This extends the range of work that can stay on the device while preserving the cloud for tasks and hardware that need it. The diagram shows the shift from cloud-first AI to everyday local tasks and then more complex local work. Its colored areas are schematic, not measured usage shares. Where Cloud AI Still Fits Hardware constraints still determine which model fits. Compute capacity, heat, and battery life matter: Edge0-35B runs on phones, while Edge0-145B runs on suitably equipped laptops. A very low-compute device cannot currently run a 145B model locally. It needs a smaller model suited to its hardware or cloud access to a model of that size. Cross-device long-term memory and searches requiring highly current information still require cloud services. Local and cloud models can work together; the appropriate split depends on the task, the hardware, and the information it needs. The aim is to make local execution a practical choice for demanding work, with a capable model that can keep working close to the person using it. That is the next step toward our goal of enabling intelligence at zero distance for everybody. Get Started with Edge0 Download the models to run locally, evaluate or fine-tune them, and build them into your own products: Model weights: Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B on Hugging Face. Inference framework and deployment guides: Edge0 on GitHub . Try it without environment setup: Download the Edge0 App . Its core model capabilities work offline, without an account or usage quota. Community: Join us on Discord . For hardware or product integrations, reach the Edge0 team through GitHub or contact@autoark.ai . FAQ What is Edge0-145B? Edge0-145B is an open-source AI model with 145 billion parameters, designed to run on personal computers. It offers capabilities like coding and reasoning, comparable to cloud models, but operates locally. How does Edge0-145B handle large models on personal hardware? Edge0-145B can run on a compatible laptop with 29GB peak memory and generates over 80 tokens per second. It uses shared matrices and efficient memory management to handle large models locally. What are the benefits of using Edge0-145B locally? Using Edge0-145B locally eliminates cloud-model fees, keeps data on your device, and maintains functionality offline. It supports complex tasks like coding and 3D modeling without relying on cloud infrastructure. Can Edge0-145B perform complex tasks? Yes, Edge0-145B can handle complex tasks such as coding, 3D modeling, and game development. It plans, executes, and iterates on tasks locally, making it suitable for demanding workflows. How does Edge0-145B compare to cloud models? Edge0-145B is competitive with specific cloud models in coding, reasoning, and instruction-following benchmarks. It offers similar capabilities while running locally, avoiding cloud-related costs and delays. What hardware is required to run Edge0-145B? Edge0-145B requires a compatible laptop with at least 29GB of memory and supports platforms like macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA RTX platforms. title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
body_text: Smart home devices should work without the internet — Do Code That Matters Do Code That Matters Blog About Do Code That Matters Blog About Smart home devices should work without the internet Oct 2026 · 3748 words · 19 min read · Spencer Kittleson Your browser does not support the audio element. Download audio Scissors cutting an ethernet cable under the words No Internet, No Problem. AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own. Secondary note: From HN, I know you don’t like AI written content so I’ve reworked most of this post to be written in my own words. The slide decks are the most interesting, LLMs were used to add context. I’m making those available as downloads for first talk and then second talk . TLDR; Every core smart device in my house does not depend on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, everything works (downgraded experience perhaps). It has been my rule for 10 years and it has been challenging to follow. I’ve given two talks about it. Check out each slide by slide. Why local My Nest integration worked one day until it didn’t. They had changed the api (around the same time Google acquired them). I have a few more examples in these talks that show a samsung fridge and a grill controller that needs wifi to show temperature. I don’t/shouldn’t need wifi and/or vendor service to interact with hardware. So everything that matters runs on hardware I own. Mostly on Tasmota on esp8266/esp32 boards, MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services for enhancements like Alexa and a few AWS ones BUT those are secondary. If the internet is down, the switches all work like normal. The rules From the first talk: No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. Be agile. Check your automations. Exceptions must be exceptional. Added after year five, once more people lived in the house: A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. Configuration lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. More than one way to do something. An app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. If I keep doing the same steps, it becomes routine (node red or on the tasmota device itself). Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. I get asked about the the Tasmota sprinkler controller the most as well as the garage door setup. Both have been running for years with no real changes. Talk One: Home Automation Nobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background. Each automation is a small puzzle. Its a hobby. Everything seems to want to reach out to the cloud. Laptops, phones, etc make sense. However my thermostats and locks… smart devices need to be questioned since they could be critical useful in your home. They may go out of business so be mindful what your signing up. Many start start with these devices: thermostat, smart plug, smart lock. Each can have its own account and app. Usually people will try to combine devices into the same ecosystem when possible. Know this triangle: cloud cam is cheap and easy but in exchange for costs you privacy. A smart plug I flash myself takes longer to set up, but I can hook it into anything. Figure out where a device lands before buying it. This is bad behavior. Don’t tape switches to the on position. The better fix is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch. It still works like a normal switch and I can automate it. More work to install than a smart plug. Nobody has to change their habits. Rule one: if the internet goes down, my lights still turn on. Being agile means willing to understand that changes will come that you must in your system. A small workflow to keep my garage cool in the summer time. I’ve had to change it multiple times. I have a reed switch wired up to the tasmota esp32 that controls the garage door with global state. I use grafana to monitor the state changes. I want to know if the garage door was left open so i could get message to me that its been open for too long. Scheduled triggers on a single pump. Be careful here, automations fighting over one device can happen and has caused me problems. Make it a habit to check every so often. Broken many of these rules so now i refer to them as guidelines! Three ways to do “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style applets cover the stuff I don’t want to build myself. MQTT keeps things decoupled as a pub sub event system. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening. So a phone and a backend can both subscribe without the sensor doing anything extra. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post works the same way. A Sonoff Mini fits inside the fireplace wiring, and the dashboard or Alexa can flip it. A fake fire you can turn on by voice is a good party trick. The whole sprinkler build: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware. It’s a bit hacky but I love it :D Talk one in five lines. The one I break most is the first, don’t introduce a new way while removing the old one, and I regret it every time. The last one stops me from breaking the others for no good reason. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count. That was talk one. Most of the “memorable automations” later broke in some new way or got replaced, so there’s a sequel. Talk Two: Home Automation, The Sequel Enough time passed between the talks that I had a new list of problems. More devices means more decisions made without me. It’s a little unsettling but mostly harmless. Everyone else is dealing with this too from what I can see. The same rules from talk one (worded a bit tighter). The rules stayed the same but more were added. My setup assumed one person lived in the house. More people meant traffic pattern differences and additional access keys. Also, I would be longer away. So I needed two additional systems water flooding detection and presence detection. Same joke, new rules. These are rules 6 to 11 at the top of the post. Now the builds! A motor and PVC pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped to a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for sanitizing. Random automations with a water pump, AirGradient kit, and robot vacuum. This dashboard replaced more apps than anything else: garage door, side door unlock, front lock, all lights on or off, brightness, a coffee bar color picker, and warm-to-cool for the living room. It’s one cheap tablet next to the thermostat. No one needs an app. Its a physical device everyone can go to if needed. The lights behind the TV run through the same system instead of their own remote. These lights turn on when the TV comes on. Shuts off at smart times as well. I do recommend smart locks when you need to have access controls in places other than just keys. Check out the parts at the end of this post to see what I have used. The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom (it’s cheap). I’ve been able to find smart plugs I can flash with Tasmota. The Raspberry Pi 2 B runs Node-RED and Grafana. LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely. The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing. Node-RED for the logic, Grafana to see what’s happening, Tasmota on anything I flash, Telegram for notifications, and Python or JavaScript for glue code that doesn’t fit in a flow. My Garage flow today. It’s crazy but it works and gets changed often. This is the “is everything okay” dashboard: humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure and gas on one side, and energy use, door opens and on-status history on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing. Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on. The “more than one way in” rule in hardware: the wall tablet for whoever is standing there, NFC tags and a QR code to tap, and an Echo Dot for anyone who would rather talk to the house. The tools I build and debug all of this with. That’s both talks five years apart. The rules barely changed, just extended. The list of problems kept growing. A third talk is coming around agentic use cases. The same rules should hold when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches. I expect to add a few more rules in the process. What Readers are telling me I shared this post on LinkedIn and Hacker News and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Summarizations of those thoughts: Everyone has one Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server: A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app. A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail. A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network. A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant. A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network. Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling. Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates. A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business. The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company. It stopped working anyway. Rules readers added Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own. Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection. Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed. A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone. Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker. Practical tips Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet. Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box. Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats. Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away. Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale. There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that. Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation , which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought. Counterpoints Internet connectivity has real cases that are obvious, such as a meat thermometer that lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. Remote access to systems where you really need them such as cameras. Devices I’ve used (This section has Amazon affiliate links. If you buy through them, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) These are the parts from my home automation builds, grouped by project. Sprinkler controller Gear Purpose Buy HiLetgo ESP8266 NodeMCU board (3 pack) Wi-Fi microcontroller that runs Tasmota Amazon SSD1306 OLED screen Status display for the sprinkler state Amazon Inkbird SSR-40DA solid state relay Switches the 24 VAC sprinkler valve Amazon BME280 sensor Temperature, humidity and pressure Amazon 24 VAC power supply Powers the sprinkler valve Amazon Lights, switches and plugs Gear Purpose Buy Martin Jerry smart dimmer switch (Tasmota pre-flashed) Wall light switch that runs Tasmota out of the box Amazon Martin Jerry humidity fan switch Runs the bathroom fan when humidity gets too high Amazon Sonoff S31 smart plug Power watchdog for the cable modem Amazon Serial-to-USB adapter Connects an ESP8266 to your PC for flashing Tasmota Amazon Garage door Gear Purpose Buy Raspberry Pi 3 Runs Docker and the web API Amazon SunFounder 2-channel 5V relay module Simulates the button press to toggle the door Amazon LiftMaster wired control panel (78LM, replaces the 41A5273-1) Bypasses the anti-tamper wiring Amazon Around the house Gear Purpose Buy GL.iNet Flint 2 router (GL-MT6000) Runs OpenWrt and an MQTT broker locally Amazon Cheap tablet Mounted on the wall as the dashboard Amazon Lefant robot vacuum Cleans the floors Amazon See something inaccurate or need more detail? title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
body_text: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG - Apple Machine Learning Research Machine Learning Research Open Menu Close Menu Overview Research Highlights Publications Events Work with us content type highlight published November 5, 2026 Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution â a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs â rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs â is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently. In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions , a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) â once, offline, for a fixed database of keys â that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs. The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters â k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n â keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n / k â a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below. Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid. MIPS as a Support Function What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs) . Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself. The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input. Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best: The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality. KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Eulerâs theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced. Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter. Learned Routing with SupportNet As shown in Figure 1 , the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each clusterâs centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match. If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2 , in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings. Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each clusterâs support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster. Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: âHow good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?â SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values. Figure 3: SupportNets approximate the support functions of each cluster and assign queries to clusters based on the best match with any key, not only centroids as typical geometric approaches do. We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup. Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top- s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, â¦, 128) . Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters. The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9Ã faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids. The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90â93% of the time â up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) â versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline. SupportNet Router Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 4: Routing performance (recall) due to SupportNets of various sizes versus latency or the fraction of the database we allow the router to scan. Routers, all with a depth of 16 layers, are trained on a 128-cluster Natural Questions dataset. SupportNets dominate the centroid router: given a latency target, one can get a higher recall with a SupportNet or conversely, that recall can be achieved at lower latency by a SupportNet than by a centroid router. Plugging Into Existing Indices SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a âquery rewriterâ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5 : sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association. Figure 5: KeyNets are trained to map a query to its best match in a database. Combined with an IVF index, pre-processing queries via such a mapping makes search much easier: the resulting transformed query is now much closer to the target it is intended to retrieve. We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recallâcost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8Ã less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in âqualityâ provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89â97% of the time â up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) â versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11Ã fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it. KeyNet Searcher Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 6: Search performance (recall) using an IVF index to search a database made from the Natural Questions dataset. The plots compare results due to querying the IVF index directly with raw queries against a search executed after mapping queries with KeyNets of various sizes, all with a fixed depth of 16 layers. Latency in the plots corresponds to the total time required to map a query and search, except for the raw-query case, which accounts only for search. Pre-processing queries with KeyNet is worth it no matter the size: the pre-processing overhead is compensated for by faster search downstream. We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNetâs predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep. Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query. Gallery item 1 Gallery item 2 Gallery item 3 Gallery item 4 Gallery item 5 Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is Matchbox Twenty?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'Who wrote The Eye of the World?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is a wind controller used for?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When will the Summertime Ball be on?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When was the show Victorious on Nickelodeon?' Which Network Should You Use? The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes â a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster. A New Direction for Learned Retrieval Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance â a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called amortization ) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve. Related readings and updates. Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions July 2, 2026 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICML Maximum inner product search (MIPS) is a crucial subroutine in machine learning, requiring the identification of a vector taken within a database (the keys) that best aligns with a given query. We propose amortized MIPS: a regression-based approach that trains neural networks to directly predict MIPS solutions, amortizing the cost of repeatedly solving MIPS for queries drawn from a known distribution over a fixed key database. Our key insight isâ¦ Read more Scalable Private Search with Wally October 16, 2024 research area Privacy This paper presents Wally, a private search system that supports efficient semantic and keyword search queries against large databases. When sufficiently many clients are making queries, Wallyâs performance is significantly better than previous systems. In previous private search systems, for each client query, the server must perform at least one expensive cryptographic operation per database entry. As a result, performance degradedâ¦ Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning. Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day. A free, open-source alternative to Granola. Download for Mac · Windows · Linux Yogurt records your calls without adding a bot to the meeting. macOS 14.4+ (Apple Silicon) · Windows 10 2004+ (x64) · Ubuntu 22.04+ or similar (x64 AppImage) · 8 GB memory yogurt.so · Help · Build and run locally · MIT license Made by Frigade . What it does Live transcripts. Yogurt records calls and turns speech into text as you talk. Meeting summaries. Yogurt writes up the conversation and any notes you add. Private by default. Your audio, transcripts and AI processing stay on your computer. Free and open source. You can use Yogurt without an account. Who said what. Yogurt names speakers from Zoom, Teams and Meet on Mac only. Languages. Multi-language mode transcribes 99 languages. Recording reminders. Yogurt offers to record when a supported call starts. Answers with sources. Yogurt answers questions across meetings and links to the source. Folders and search. You can find meetings by folder, title, notes or transcript. Copy and export. You can copy notes or transcripts, or save both as Markdown. Local MCP server. Your chosen assistant app can read your notes when you allow access. Automatic stop. Yogurt stops recording when the call ends. Watch the demo yogurt-demo.mp4 How it works Record. Start recording your microphone and call audio; you can add your own notes. Transcribe. Yogurt uses whisper.cpp and, on supported Macs, Apple SpeechAnalyzer. Summarize and ask. A local open-weight model runs through llama.cpp. Meeting data stays local; Yogurt goes online for model downloads and update checks. Where your meetings, recordings, settings and models are stored Mac uses ~/Library/Application Support/Yogurt . Windows uses %APPDATA%\Yogurt . Linux uses ~/.config/Yogurt , or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Yogurt if set. FAQ What kind of computer do I need? A Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 14.4 or newer, a 64-bit PC with Windows 10 (version 2004) or newer, or a 64-bit Linux computer with Ubuntu 22.04 or newer. Each needs at least 8 GB of memory. If your computer is too slow, Yogurt tells you during setup. Calendar and speaker names from calls are Mac only for now. Windows says “Windows protected your PC.” What do I do? Click More info, then Run anyway. Windows shows this for new apps that aren’t signed with a Microsoft certificate yet. Yogurt is open source, so anyone can check what it does. Does Yogurt join my meetings? No. Yogurt records your microphone and the sound playing on your computer. No bot joins the call, so let the other people on the call know you’re recording. Are recordings saved? Yes. Your recordings, transcripts, and notes are saved locally on your computer. Is Yogurt free? Yes. Yogurt is free and open source under the MIT license. No account is needed. Does Yogurt work offline? Yes. After a one-time download of the AI models, transcription and summaries run locally on your computer. How much does setup download? It depends on your computer. Yogurt downloads a smaller notes model first, about 5 GB, then the best one your computer can run well, which can be 14 GB or more. Recording works once setup finishes, and notes and questions work offline once the notes model is in. How do I connect my assistant app? In Settings → AI apps , turn on access, copy the helper command, and add it as a local MCP server in your assistant app. Access is off by default. The app can read your meetings, notes and transcripts, but cannot change them. It may send what it reads to its own online model. Turn access off in Yogurt to stop further reads. Can other apps read my notes through MCP? Access is off until you enable it in Settings → AI apps . Apps get read-only access to meetings, notes and transcripts. Mac and Linux use a socket in your profile folder with 0600 permissions, so only your user account can open it. Windows uses a named pipe with a new random name each launch, stored only in your profile folder. There is no per-app token, so any app running under your account can read while access is on. Settings shows connected apps by their self-reported names. Which AI models does Yogurt use? Transcription uses Whisper through whisper.cpp, with large-v3-turbo or a smaller model depending on your computer. On supported Macs, Apple SpeechAnalyzer supplies live words while Whisper produces the saved transcript. Summaries and answers use a local open-weight model from the Gemma 4, gpt-oss or Qwen3 families, chosen for your hardware and run through llama.cpp. The app uses Electron and needs no account. Which languages does Yogurt support? Pick Multi-language in Settings → Language → Spoken language to transcribe 99 languages. You can also switch from the English menu in a note’s footer before or during recording. English only is the default. Summaries follow the meeting’s main language; answers follow your question’s language. Settings also offers 32 app languages. Which call apps does Yogurt work with? You can record calls in any app because Yogurt captures your microphone and system audio. Call detection covers Zoom, Teams and Meet. On Mac, Yogurt can also read their speaker names with Accessibility permission, when the call app shows who is speaking. How does Yogurt know a call has started? It checks which apps are using your microphone. For browser calls, it also checks the tab title or a nearby calendar event with a call link. This triggers an offer to record; recording starts only when you choose to. How do I connect my calendar? On Mac, allow Calendar access in Settings. Yogurt reads the calendars already on your computer and lets you choose which ones to show. You do not sign into a calendar account in Yogurt.
